tool: Docker Desktop — Containers view (list, row actions, Compose grouping, single-container detail tabs, Stats sparklines, search/filter)
one_liner: A desktop dashboard that turns a potentially huge, noisy set of containers into a scannable, status-coded, group-collapsible LIST where each row reveals start/stop/inspect actions on hover and expands into a tabbed detail pane (Logs / Inspect / Exec / Files / Stats) - the canonical "list of services you start/stop/inspect" pattern PortPilot is reaching for.

ui_patterns.pattern: Persistent left nav rail with object-type sections (not top-tabs)
ui_patterns.description: A narrow vertical rail pinned on the left lists the major object types - Containers, Images, Volumes, Builds, Docker Scout, Extensions, plus Settings/gear pinned at the bottom. Each is an icon + label row; the active one gets a filled background and an accent left-edge marker. It never scrolls away and never competes for horizontal width with the content table.
ui_patterns.why_not_flat: A vertical rail scales to 8-10+ destinations without eating content width or wrapping, and visually separates 'which kind of thing am I looking at' (rail) from 'which specific thing' (list) - two levels of hierarchy that horizontal top-tabs collapse into one crowded row.

ui_patterns.pattern: Dense table-row list with a leading status dot, not a card grid
ui_patterns.description: Containers render as full-width rows in a table: a colored status dot + state word at the left (green filled = Running, grey/hollow = Exited/Stopped, amber = Starting/Restarting, red = Error/Dead), then Name (bold) with image:tag in muted text beneath, then columns for status/uptime ('Running (24 minutes ago)'), port mappings rendered as clickable 'host:container' links, CPU%, and last-started. Rows are ~40px tall and zebra-free but separated by hairline dividers.
ui_patterns.why_not_flat: The leading status dot is a pre-attentive cue: you scan a single left column of colors and instantly separate running from stopped without reading any text. A uniform card grid (PortPilot's current wall) forces you to read every box; a row list with a status column lets the eye filter by color first, text second.

ui_patterns.pattern: Hover-revealed inline action cluster on each row
ui_patterns.description: Action icons live at the far right of each row and are dimmed/hidden until you hover that row, then appear as a tight horizontal cluster: Start (play ▶) OR Stop (square ■) depending on state, Restart (circular arrow), Delete (trash), plus a kebab '⋯' overflow for less-common actions (Pause, Copy docker run, View details, Open in terminal). The primary action (open the container's mapped port in a browser) is a separate prominent button.
ui_patterns.why_not_flat: Actions are contextual to row state (you only ever see Start OR Stop, never both), and hiding them until hover keeps the resting state calm and scannable instead of a wall of always-on buttons on every card. PortPilot currently shows a copy icon + red X on all 33 cards at once, which is visual noise multiplied by 33.

ui_patterns.pattern: Compose project as a collapsible parent row with nested children
ui_patterns.description: Containers started by the same Docker Compose project collapse under a single bold parent row showing the project name and an aggregate state ('Running 3/3'), with a disclosure chevron (▸/▾). Expanding indents the child container rows beneath it with a connecting tree line. The parent row carries group-level actions (Start all / Stop all / Delete all) that fan out to every child. Standalone containers sit at the top level, ungrouped.
ui_patterns.why_not_flat: This is two-level grouping inside one list: the parent gives you a roll-up (one line per app), children give detail on demand. It is exactly the 'separate signal from noise / group related things' move PortPilot needs - and it lets you act on a whole app (stop all) without touching unrelated containers.

ui_patterns.pattern: Expand-row-into-detail via full-page drill-down with a tabbed sub-view
ui_patterns.description: Clicking a row navigates into a dedicated detail page for that one container (with a breadcrumb back to the list). The detail page header repeats the name, status dot, and the same action cluster, and below it a horizontal tab strip switches the lower pane between Logs, Inspect, Bind mounts, Exec (or Debug), Files, and Stats - without leaving the container's context.
ui_patterns.why_not_flat: Master-detail adds a whole second level of depth that a flat grid has nowhere to put: the list answers 'what exists and what state is it in', the detail answers 'what is this one doing right now'. Tabs further subdivide the detail so logs, config, and metrics don't all pile onto one scroll.

ui_patterns.pattern: Stats tab with live resource sparklines/area charts
ui_patterns.description: The Stats tab shows live-updating area/line charts for CPU %, Memory usage (with a used/limit number like '128MB / 512MB'), Network I/O, and Disk read/write, each a small labeled chart with the current value called out as a big number above its trend line. They animate in real time while the container runs.
ui_patterns.why_not_flat: A number plus its recent trendline encodes 'is this healthy / spiking / idle' in a glance - depth of information per row that a static label can't carry. It turns 'running' from a binary into a living signal.

ui_patterns.pattern: Top search/filter bar plus state filter chips
ui_patterns.description: Above the list sits a single Search field (filters by name as you type) alongside a state filter (Running / Stopped / All) and a 'Only show running containers' toggle, so the table can be narrowed by text and by status independently. The result count and bulk-select checkbox live in the same header strip.
ui_patterns.why_not_flat: Filtering by status is the mechanism that lets one list hold both noise and signal: the default 'only running' view hides the dozens of stopped/system rows so you see just your live work, then you opt into the full set when you need it. PortPilot's flat 33-card wall has a text filter but no status filter, so OS noise is always present.

ui_patterns.pattern: Header bulk-select with batch action toolbar
ui_patterns.description: A checkbox in the list header (and per row on hover) selects multiple containers; selecting any row swaps the header into a contextual action bar ('3 selected · Start · Stop · Delete') so you can operate on many at once. Clearing the selection restores the normal header.
ui_patterns.why_not_flat: Bulk operations on a selection are impossible in a card grid of individual action buttons - the selection model adds an interaction layer that treats the list as a set, not 33 isolated objects.

ui_patterns.pattern: Port mappings rendered as live clickable links
ui_patterns.description: In the row's Ports column, each published port shows as 'host_port:container_port' and the host part is a hyperlink that opens http://localhost:host_port in the browser; an external-link icon appears on hover.
ui_patterns.why_not_flat: The port stops being a static label and becomes the primary 'go to my app' affordance, tying the list row directly to the thing the user actually wants (the running app in a browser).

steal_these.idea: Convert the Active Ports two-column card grid into a single dense row-list with a leading status dot per row
steal_these.how: Each port becomes a ~40px row: status dot (green = a tracked dev server, grey = system/OS port, amber = starting) + ':PORT' + process/PID + truncated command, with hover-revealed copy/kill actions at the right. The color column lets the eye separate the user's :3000/:3001 dev servers from svchost/:135/:445 noise instantly - killing the 'wall of 33 equal boxes' problem directly.

steal_these.idea: Group ports/containers under collapsible parent rows: 'My dev servers', 'System / OS ports', and per-project Compose-style groups
steal_these.how: Mirror Compose nesting. Auto-classify scanned ports into a 'System / OS' collapsible group (collapsed by default, with a count like 'System ports (28) ▸') and surface the user's registered/dev ports at the top. Where several ports belong to one registered app, nest them under that app's parent row with a 'Running 2/2' roll-up. This is the single highest-value move for the 'flatness' complaint.

steal_these.idea: Add a status filter / 'only show my dev servers' toggle next to the existing text filter
steal_these.how: Beside the current filter input and '33 ports' badge, add chips (All / My apps / Dev ports / System) and default to hiding the System group. Same mechanism Docker uses ('only show running') to keep noise out of the default view while keeping it one click away.

steal_these.idea: Merge My Apps and Active Ports into one master list where a registered app row shows its live port inline
steal_these.how: Stop splitting 'is it running / on which port' across two tabs. Make one list where each registered app is a parent row carrying a live status dot, its current PID/port (pulled from the active scan), start/stop controls, and - if it spawns multiple listeners - nested child port rows. Unregistered live ports appear as a separate ungrouped section below. One surface answers both questions Docker answers in its Containers view.

steal_these.idea: Replace static per-row info with an expand-to-detail pane with tabs (Logs / Info / Stats)
steal_these.how: Clicking a port/app row opens a detail panel (right-side drawer or drill-down) with the action cluster in the header and tabs: Logs (tail the dev server's stdout if PortPilot manages the process), Info (full command, cwd, env, PID tree - PortPilot's 'Inspect'), and Stats (CPU/mem sparkline for the PID). This gives the depth a flat card can't hold and a reason for rows to stay compact.

steal_these.idea: Adopt a left nav rail instead of horizontal top-tabs
steal_these.how: Move ACTIVE PORTS / MY APPS (or the merged list) / KNOWLEDGE / SETTINGS into a slim left icon+label rail with the gold accent as a left-edge marker on the active item and Settings pinned at the bottom. Frees the full window width for the data-dense list and scales past 5 destinations without the gold-underline tab row wrapping.

steal_these.idea: Hover-reveal contextual action clusters; show Start XOR Stop, never both
steal_these.how: On a row, render only the action valid for its current state (a stopped app shows ▶ Start; a running one shows ■ Stop + restart + kill), revealed on hover with a kebab '⋯' for secondary actions (copy command, copy docker/run-equivalent, open in browser, reveal in finder). Calms the resting UI versus today's always-on copy+X on every one of 33 cards.

steal_these.idea: Make the port number a live clickable link that opens localhost:PORT
steal_these.how: Render ':3000' as a hyperlink that launches http://localhost:3000 with a hover external-link icon - turning the most prominent element on each row into the 'open my app' affordance instead of just a label to read.

steal_these.idea: Give Settings a left sub-nav rail instead of a flat vertical stack of bordered boxes
steal_these.how: Echo Docker Desktop Settings, which itself uses a left list (General / Resources / Docker Engine / ...) + right detail pane. PortPilot's THEME / PREFERENCES / DATA become a small left list inside the Settings surface with the form on the right - sub-hierarchy instead of three full-width stacked panels.

status_visualization: Status is carried almost entirely by a single leading status dot per row plus a one-word state label, read pre-attentively down the left column: green filled = Running, hollow/grey = Exited/Stopped, amber = Starting/Restarting/Paused, red = Error/Dead. The state is reinforced by which inline action appears (Stop on running, Start on stopped) and by an uptime phrase ('Running (24 minutes ago)'). On the detail Stats tab, status deepens into live CPU/Memory/Network/Disk sparklines with a big current-value number over a trend line, so 'running' becomes a health signal (idle vs spiking) rather than a binary. Compose parent rows show an aggregate roll-up like 'Running 3/3'. For PortPilot, the dot-color column is the key transplant: it is what lets a single list hold both the user's live dev servers and OS noise while remaining instantly separable - the exact fix for the flat, uniform-box complaint.
density_and_hierarchy: Docker keeps a large container set manageable through four stacked techniques rather than one flat grid: (1) collapsible Compose parent rows roll many containers into one line with a count, expandable on demand - master-detail at the list level; (2) a default 'only running' filter plus a Search field hides the long tail of stopped/system rows so the resting view shows only what matters; (3) compact ~40px table rows with a status-dot column and muted secondary text (image:tag under the bold name) pack high information density while staying scannable; (4) drill-down detail pages with tabs (Logs/Inspect/Exec/Files/Stats) move per-item depth OUT of the row entirely, so the list stays terse and the detail stays rich. Hierarchy comes from three real levels - nav rail (object type) → grouped/filtered list (which item) → tabbed detail (what it's doing) - exactly the depth PortPilot's two-tab, single-grid layout lacks. The direct lesson: hierarchy is created by grouping + filtering + master-detail, not by styling cards.
caveats: Do not copy Docker's full-page drill-down navigation wholesale - PortPilot is smaller, so a right-side detail drawer that keeps the list visible is lighter than Docker's breadcrumb page swap and avoids a back-button maze. Do not import the entire detail tab set; Logs/Inspect/Stats map cleanly but Bind mounts, Files (container filesystem browser), and Exec/Debug (shell into a container) have no honest equivalent for a host-process port manager - faking them would be empty UI. The Stats sparkline is desirable but only if PortPilot owns the process and can sample its PID's CPU/mem; for ports it merely scanned (svchost, System PID 4) there's no managed process to chart, so reserve Stats for registered apps PortPilot started, not arbitrary OS ports. Don't over-build bulk-select if single-port kill is the dominant action - add it only once grouping makes 'stop all in this group' meaningful. Finally, Docker Desktop's chrome is fairly heavy and neutral-grey; PortPilot already has strong per-theme palettes (TokyoNight, Dracula, etc.), so adopt Docker's structure and information hierarchy, not its visual styling - let the existing CSS-variable themes carry the look.
applicability_reason: Docker Desktop's Containers view is almost a one-to-one structural analog of PortPilot - a list of host-bound services you start/stop/inspect, with grouping (Compose ≈ projects), per-row status, inline lifecycle actions, port links, and master-detail - so its grouped-collapsible-list + status-dot + filter + drill-down patterns map onto PortPilot's exact flatness problem with very little translation loss, the only gaps being container-specific tabs (Files/Exec/Bind mounts) that don't fit a port manager.

one_liner: A native Swift macOS app that manages Docker containers, Compose projects, Kubernetes, and Linux VMs through a single source-list sidebar plus a tabbed detail pane, using OS-native controls and quiet status dots to feel like a Finder/Mail-class system app rather than a dashboard.

ui_patterns.pattern: macOS source-list sidebar with collapsible section headers
ui_patterns.description: The left rail is a native NSOutlineView-style 'source list' (the same control Finder/Mail/Music use): a narrow, slightly translucent column with uppercase gray group headers - Containers, Images, Volumes, Kubernetes, Linux Machines, plus a Docker section. Each header has a disclosure triangle and a live count. Selecting a row swaps the whole right pane. The sidebar is the single spine of navigation; there are no top tabs eating vertical space.
ui_patterns.why_not_flat: Replaces a flat tab bar with a hierarchical tree that has named, countable, collapsible groups. Hierarchy is structural (sidebar = sections, content = detail) rather than everything-on-one-plane, and it scales to many more sections than a horizontal tab strip ever could.

ui_patterns.pattern: Compose-project grouping with parent rows and indented children
ui_patterns.description: Containers are not a flat list - they nest under their Docker Compose project as a collapsible parent row. The project row shows an aggregate status (e.g. a green dot if all services up, amber/mixed if partial) and a count like '3 containers'; expanding it reveals the indented member containers (web, db, redis) each with their own dot. Standalone containers sit at the same indent level as projects but without children.
ui_patterns.why_not_flat: This is the single biggest anti-flatness move: it turns N equal rows into a two-level tree where the meaningful unit (the project / app) is the parent and the noise (individual sidecar containers) collapses away. Exactly the my-app-to-its-running-processes relationship PortPilot is missing.

ui_patterns.pattern: Quiet colored status dot as the primary state glyph
ui_patterns.description: State is carried by a small filled circle at the left of each row: green = running, gray/hollow = stopped, amber = starting/unhealthy/partial, red = error/exited-nonzero. The dot is ~8px, muted (not neon), and consistent across sidebar rows, the menu-bar popover, and the detail header. Secondary metadata (uptime '2h', CPU%, image tag) sits in dimmed gray trailing text.
ui_patterns.why_not_flat: A flat wall has no visual sort key; the dot gives every row an instant scannable state channel so the eye groups 'green things' and 'gray things' pre-attentively without reading text. Color does the grouping that layout alone can't.

ui_patterns.pattern: Tabbed detail pane: Info / Logs / Terminal / Files
ui_patterns.description: Selecting a container fills the right pane with a header (name, status dot, image, primary Start/Stop/Restart buttons) and a native segmented-control tab bar: Info (ports, env, mounts, networks as labeled key/value rows), Logs (live-tailing colorized stream with a search field), Terminal (one-click shell into the container), Files (a Finder-like browser of the container filesystem). Switching containers keeps the same tab selected.
ui_patterns.why_not_flat: Creates depth via master-detail: the list stays lightweight while all the rich, per-item data lives one click deeper in a consistent tabbed surface. Daily actions (read logs, exec a shell) become UI affordances instead of remembered CLI, and the list never has to carry that weight.

ui_patterns.pattern: Row-level hover actions plus a primary inline toggle
ui_patterns.description: Each sidebar/list row exposes controls only on hover or selection: a start/stop toggle, a '...' overflow menu (restart, delete, copy ID, open in browser), and for web services a small globe/open-in-browser button. Resting rows stay clean - just dot, name, and dimmed metadata. The most common action (start/stop) is a single affordance, not a menu dive.
ui_patterns.why_not_flat: Progressive disclosure: actions appear contextually instead of every row carrying a permanent cluster of buttons (PortPilot's current copy+kill on all 33 cards). The default visual weight per row drops dramatically, so density goes up without clutter.

ui_patterns.pattern: Menu-bar applet as a condensed mirror of the sidebar
ui_patterns.description: The menu-bar icon (a small orb that subtly reflects overall state) opens a compact NSMenu/popover listing your projects and containers with the same status dots and inline start/stop/open-web actions. It's the 80%-case control surface - flip a service on, hit its URL - without opening the main window. It groups by project just like the main app.
ui_patterns.why_not_flat: Demonstrates a second, denser representation of the same hierarchy for glanceability. The same grouped model renders at two altitudes (full window vs menubar), proving the data model carries the hierarchy, not the layout.

ui_patterns.pattern: Categorized Settings in a native preferences window
ui_patterns.description: Settings open in a separate, smaller native window (not an in-app tab) organized into categories - System, Docker, Kubernetes, Network, and an Advanced bucket for power/CLI-only toggles. Each category is a short page of native controls (toggles, steppers, segmented pickers) with inline helper subtext, mirroring macOS System Settings conventions.
ui_patterns.why_not_flat: Splits a long config stack into named categories so the common toggles aren't buried under advanced ones. Native controls + helper subtext give each setting hierarchy (label / control / explanation) instead of a flat run of bordered boxes.

ui_patterns.pattern: Native typography, spacing, and translucency restraint ('beautiful' = system-native, not custom-skinned)
ui_patterns.description: Reviewers call it beautiful largely because it looks like Apple built it: SF Pro system font, standard macOS row heights and inset spacing, sidebar vibrancy/translucency, hairline separators, and almost no custom chrome or brand color. State and structure carry the design; there is no heavy theme, no gradient cards, no oversized accent text.
ui_patterns.why_not_flat: The hierarchy comes from disciplined typographic scale and whitespace (group header vs row vs dimmed metadata) rather than borders around everything. Restraint is what makes a dense list readable - the opposite of 33 equally-weighted bordered cards.

steal_these.idea: Two-level grouped list: 'My Apps' as parent rows, their live ports/processes as indented children, in ONE unified view
steal_these.how: Merge Active Ports and My Apps into a single source-list. Each registered app is a parent row with an aggregate status dot (green if its expected port is live, gray if stopped); expanding it reveals the actual listening port(s)/PID it currently owns, pulled from the scan. This directly fixes the 'is my app running and on which port' split across two tabs - it becomes one expandable row.

steal_these.idea: Signal-vs-noise grouping for the port wall: 'My Dev Servers' / 'Other Project Ports' / 'System & OS Ports' sections
steal_these.how: Replace the uniform 33-card grid with a grouped, collapsible list. Ports matching a registered app go in 'My Dev Servers' (top, expanded). Unrecognized user ports (3000-9000 range, node/python/etc) go in 'Other'. OS/system ports (:135 svchost, :139/:445 System PID 4) collapse into a 'System & OS' section that's collapsed by default. The noise is one disclosure-triangle away, never gone, never equal-weighted with real dev servers.

steal_these.idea: Status dot as the universal left-edge glyph across all three surfaces
steal_these.how: Adopt one 8px filled-circle convention: green=listening/running, gray=stopped/registered-but-down, amber=starting or port-conflict, red=kill-failed/error. Use it on every desktop row, the VS Code tree items (TreeItem.iconPath with themed color), and the menu-bar/status-bar counter. One glyph language across Electron, extension, and web portal.

steal_these.idea: Replace the KNOWLEDGE top-tab with a master-detail right pane and a tabbed port/app detail
steal_these.how: Drop KNOWLEDGE as a primary tab. Make the right pane a detail surface: clicking a port/app shows a header (port, process, status dot, Stop/Kill/Open-in-browser buttons) plus tabs - Info (PID, full command, cwd, env), Logs (if the app was started by PortPilot, tail its stdout), and Open (the localhost URL). The truncated COMMAND line currently crammed into every card moves here, decluttering the list.

steal_these.idea: Source-list sidebar instead of horizontal top-tabs
steal_these.how: Move ACTIVE PORTS / MY APPS / SETTINGS from a gold-underlined top tab strip to a left sidebar with section headers and counts (e.g. 'Dev Servers 5', 'System 28'). This reclaims vertical space, scales past 5 destinations, and gives the app the native master-detail spine OrbStack uses. Active selection is a filled sidebar row, not an underline.

steal_these.idea: Hover-only row actions to kill PortPilot's permanent per-card button clutter
steal_these.how: Show only the status dot + port + process at rest; reveal copy, kill, and open-in-browser on row hover/selection, with rarer actions behind a '...' overflow. This lets rows shrink from chunky two-column cards to a dense single-column list where 33 ports are scannable without 66 always-on buttons.

steal_these.idea: Categorized settings with inline helper subtext instead of a flat stack of bordered boxes
steal_these.how: Keep settings as a section but split into named groups - Appearance (the 6 themes as a segmented/swatch picker), Scanning (auto-scan toggle + interval stepper with 'How often to re-scan ports' subtext), Data (export/import). Each control gets a label + native control + one dimmed helper line, mirroring macOS System Settings, rather than three equal full-width boxes.

status_visualization: OrbStack's entire state model rides on one quiet, consistent glyph: a small (~8px) filled colored dot at the left edge of every row - green=running, gray/hollow=stopped, amber=starting/unhealthy/partial, red=exited-with-error. The same dot appears in the sidebar, the detail-pane header, and the menu-bar popover, so state reads identically everywhere. Crucially, parent (Compose project) rows show an AGGREGATE dot derived from their children - green when all up, amber when some down - so a collapsed project still communicates rollup health without expansion. Secondary state (uptime, CPU%, image) is dimmed gray trailing text, never competing with the dot. Colors are muted/system-toned, not neon, which keeps a dense list calm. The lesson for PortPilot: state is a pre-attentive color channel, not a textual STATUS column - and a parent row should roll up its children's state.
density_and_hierarchy: OrbStack handles many items through layering, not pagination. (1) Grouping: containers nest under Compose projects, so a screen of 30 containers collapses to ~6 project rows you expand on demand - the meaningful unit is the parent. (2) Collapsible sections: each sidebar category (Containers, Images, Volumes, K8s, Machines) is independently collapsible with a count, so you hide whole domains you don't care about. (3) Master-detail: the list stays lightweight (dot + name + dimmed metadata) because all rich data - logs, env, files, terminal - lives one click deeper in the tabbed detail pane, never inline. (4) Progressive disclosure of actions: controls appear on hover/selection, so resting rows carry almost no chrome. (5) Two altitudes: the menu-bar applet is a condensed mirror for the common case so you rarely page through the full window at all. The net effect is high information density that never reads as a wall, because the eye works top-down through named groups and colored dots rather than scanning equal boxes.
caveats: Do not copy OrbStack's macOS-nativeness literally - PortPilot's primary surface is an Electron app with CSS-variable theming (TokyoNight, Dracula, etc.), so 'beautiful = invisible system-native chrome' must be reinterpreted as 'disciplined typographic hierarchy + restraint', not 'use NSOutlineView'. Don't adopt translucency/vibrancy; it won't read the same cross-theme and can hurt contrast on the Brutalist Light theme. OrbStack's Compose-project grouping is clean because Docker hands it an explicit project label - PortPilot has no equivalent ground truth linking a scanned port to a registered app, so the parent/child grouping needs a heuristic (match by configured port, then by process command/cwd) and must degrade gracefully when a match is ambiguous (show the port ungrouped under 'Other', never guess wrong). A separate native Settings WINDOW is a macOS convention; for a cross-platform Electron + VS Code + web-portal product, keep settings as an in-app categorized section rather than a detached window. The four-tab detail view (esp. Logs/Terminal/Files) assumes OrbStack owns the container runtime - PortPilot only owns processes it started, so a Logs tab is only honest for PortPilot-launched apps; don't promise a terminal/file browser into arbitrary scanned PIDs. Finally, don't over-rotate on the menu-bar applet for the desktop redesign - it's a nice-to-have second altitude, not the core fix for flatness.
applicability_reason: OrbStack solves almost exactly PortPilot's stated problem - turning a flat wall of equal runtime items into a grouped, status-dotted, master-detail source list that separates signal from noise and unifies 'registered thing' with 'its live state' - so nearly every pattern maps directly onto active-ports, my-apps, navigation, and detail-view, with only the macOS-native rendering needing translation to Electron.

tool: Laravel Herd and DBngin (native macOS dev-service managers)
one_liner: Two native macOS menu-bar apps for running local dev services - Herd manages PHP sites/runtimes, DBngin manages database engines - both built on a tight row-per-service list with a single start/stop toggle and a calm, monochrome-plus-one-accent aesthetic.

ui_patterns.pattern: Menu-bar-first, window-second interaction model
ui_patterns.description: Both apps live primarily as a menu-bar icon. Herd's icon dropdown is a compact menu: a list of services with checkmarks, the current global PHP version, quick links (Open, Settings, Pause). The full window (Sites, PHP, Settings sidebar) is the 'cockpit' you open only when you need depth. DBngin's panel is a small floating window pinned near the menu bar. The cheap, frequent action (glance at status, toggle one service) happens in the lightweight surface; the expensive, rare action (configure, inspect) happens in the heavy surface.
ui_patterns.why_not_flat: Splits the UI by frequency-of-use rather than cramming every control into one always-visible plane. A glance-and-toggle layer sits above a configure-and-inspect layer, so the default view is sparse and the dense view is opt-in - the opposite of PortPilot's single flat wall.

ui_patterns.pattern: Row-per-service with one dominant start/stop toggle
ui_patterns.description: DBngin's window is a vertical list where each row = one database engine instance. The row anatomy is rigid: a colored engine glyph (MySQL dolphin blue, Postgres elephant, Redis red) on the left, then the engine name + version (e.g. 'PostgreSQL 16'), then port (e.g. '5432'), and a single large Start/Stop button pinned hard-right. There is exactly ONE primary action per row and it is the biggest, most colorful thing in the row. Secondary actions (open in TablePlus, edit, remove) are smaller or tucked into a row hover/context menu.
ui_patterns.why_not_flat: Every row has a clear visual focal point (the toggle) and a clear identity (the engine glyph + version), so the eye lands on 'what is this, and is it on?' instantly. PortPilot's cards give equal weight to PORT/PROCESS/PID/COMMAND/copy/kill - five competing elements - so nothing reads as primary. One dominant control per row is what makes a list scannable instead of a grid of equal noise.

ui_patterns.pattern: Binary status as a colored dot, not a label
ui_patterns.description: DBngin shows running state as a single small filled dot: green = running, grey = stopped. It sits adjacent to the engine name. No 'STATUS: RUNNING' text, no badge with a border. The Start button itself also flips label+color (grey 'Start' -> when running, the affordance reads as a green/active 'Stop'). Herd similarly uses a subtle secured/linked indicator per site rather than verbose status copy.
ui_patterns.why_not_flat: A pre-attentive color cue (you see green/grey before you read anything) creates an instant running/stopped axis across the whole list without adding text mass. PortPilot currently has NO status concept at all - every port looks identically 'present.' A dot column would let you scan 33 rows and find your 3 running dev servers in under a second.

ui_patterns.pattern: Inline per-row version/runtime dropdown (Herd PHP switcher)
ui_patterns.description: In Herd's Sites view, each site row carries a small inline PHP-version pill/dropdown (e.g. '8.3' that opens to 8.1/8.2/8.3/8.4). You change the runtime for that one site in place, without leaving the list or opening a modal. The global PHP version is a separate single dropdown in the menu-bar menu. So there's a clear scope hierarchy: per-row override vs. global default.
ui_patterns.why_not_flat: Puts a meaningful, frequently-changed attribute directly on the row as an interactive control, adding information density that is useful rather than decorative. It also models the global-vs-per-item scope distinction visually - something PortPilot needs for 'this app's default command' vs. 'this running instance.'

ui_patterns.pattern: Grouped / sectioned sites with collapsible headers
ui_patterns.description: Herd's newer Sites UI supports grouping: sites are organized under named group headers (by project, by folder, by team), and groups can be collapsed. There's also a 'hide sites with no valid driver' toggle to suppress noise. So the list isn't one undifferentiated column - it's sections with headers, each section collapsible to a single line.
ui_patterns.why_not_flat: Section headers introduce a second level of hierarchy (group -> item) and let you collapse whole categories you don't care about right now. This is the direct antidote to PortPilot's biggest problem: 33 equal boxes with OS noise mixed into dev signal. Group headers + collapse = signal you keep open, noise you collapse shut.

ui_patterns.pattern: Connection-detail panel revealed on demand (master-detail)
ui_patterns.description: In DBngin, clicking a database row surfaces its connection details - host, port, default username, empty password, socket path - in a detail area, often with copy-to-clipboard affordances. The list stays lean (name/version/port/toggle); the verbose metadata only appears for the selected row. It's a master-detail split, not metadata crammed onto every row.
ui_patterns.why_not_flat: Progressive disclosure: the list row carries only identity + status + primary action; everything else (the long, low-frequency fields) lives in a detail pane shown for one selected item. PortPilot currently jams the truncated COMMAND onto every card - the DBngin model would move command/PID/full-path into a detail panel and keep the row clean.

ui_patterns.pattern: Settings as a left-rail sidebar with sections, not a flat stack
ui_patterns.description: Herd's Settings is a proper preferences window: a left sidebar of categories (General, PHP, Sites, Node, Database, Services, Plugins, Licenses) with icons, and a content pane on the right that swaps per selected category. It mirrors the native macOS System Settings pattern. You navigate categories vertically in the rail; each category's controls render in the pane.
ui_patterns.why_not_flat: Two-pane settings (category rail + content) scales to many sections without an endless scroll of full-width bordered boxes. PortPilot's Settings is exactly that endless stack (Theme, Preferences, Data) - converting it to a rail+pane gives room to grow (Scanning, Groups, Integrations, Web Portal, About) without vertical bloat.

ui_patterns.pattern: Calm monochrome surface with a single semantic accent
ui_patterns.description: Both apps are visually quiet: near-white/native-grey backgrounds, thin hairline separators between rows (not heavy borders or card shadows), system font, generous-but-tight row height. Color is used SEMANTICALLY and sparingly - green for running, the brand-colored engine glyphs for identity, otherwise greyscale. There are no decorative borders around every element. The hierarchy comes from typography weight (bold engine name, lighter version/port) and the one accent, not from boxing everything.
ui_patterns.why_not_flat: Restraint creates hierarchy: when 95% of the UI is greyscale, the 5% that's colored (the green running dot, the engine glyph) carries all the meaning and pops. PortPilot's uniform blue ':PORT' on every card spends the loudest color on the least-differentiating element. Reserving color for status/identity is what makes a minimal UI read as layered rather than flat.

steal_these.idea: Add a binary green/grey status dot as the leftmost column of every port row, replacing the 'every port looks identical' flatness with an instant running/stopped axis.
steal_these.how: For PortPilot, the dot isn't just on/off - it's a category cue: green dot = my registered dev app currently listening, grey/hollow = registered app stopped, faint dot = OS/system port (noise). One pre-attentive color column lets the user scan 33 ports and find their 3 dev servers instantly, which the current uniform grid makes impossible.

steal_these.idea: Collapse the card grid into a sectioned/grouped row list with collapsible headers, separating signal from noise.
steal_these.how: Replace the two-column grid of identical cards with a single-column list grouped under headers: 'My Dev Servers' (open by default), 'Other User Ports', and a collapsed-by-default 'System / OS Ports (svchost, System PID 4, ...)'. Herd's grouped-sites + 'hide sites with no valid driver' is the exact pattern: keep signal expanded, collapse OS noise to one line. This solves the single biggest complaint (33 equal boxes) directly.

steal_these.idea: Give every row ONE dominant primary action and demote the rest to hover/detail.
steal_these.how: Mirror DBngin's one-big-button-per-row. For an Active Port row, the primary action is Kill (or Stop if it maps to a registered app); copy-PID, copy-command, and open-in-browser become small icons that appear on row hover or live in the detail panel. Right now PortPilot gives copy and kill equal top-right billing on every card, so neither reads as primary.

steal_these.idea: Merge MY APPS and ACTIVE PORTS into one master list where a registered app and its live port are the same row.
steal_these.how: DBngin's row IS the service whether it's running or not - the same row shows the configured engine and, when started, its live port and green dot. PortPilot should do the same: a registered app row shows its expected port + a Start toggle when stopped, and flips to a green dot + live PID + Stop when running. This kills the 'is my app running and on which port' split across two disconnected tabs.

steal_these.idea: Adopt a master-detail layout: lean rows on the left, a detail panel on the right for the selected item.
steal_these.how: Copy DBngin's connection-detail reveal. The row carries only identity + status + primary action; clicking it opens a right-hand panel with the full untruncated COMMAND, PID, working directory, port history, and copy buttons. This removes the truncated command line from every card (current noise) and gives a real home for the metadata PortPilot currently has nowhere to put.

steal_these.idea: Rebuild Settings as a category rail + content pane instead of a vertical stack of bordered boxes.
steal_these.how: Follow Herd's preferences-sidebar pattern: a left rail (Appearance, Scanning, Groups, Web Portal, Data, About) with the content pane on the right swapping per category. PortPilot's current flat stack (Theme / Preferences / Data) doesn't scale; the rail gives room for the new grouping rules, web-portal config, and VS Code integration settings without an endless scroll.

steal_these.idea: Replace the horizontal top-tabs with a slim left icon-rail to free vertical space and scale past 5 destinations.
steal_these.how: Herd/DBngin and native macOS apps put navigation in a vertical rail, not horizontal tabs. PortPilot's top-tabs (Active Ports | My Apps | Knowledge | Settings) eat vertical height and won't scale; a 44px left icon-rail recovers that height for the data-dense list and leaves room for future destinations (Groups, Logs) without crowding the gold-underline tab strip.

status_visualization: Binary state shown as a single small filled dot - green = running, grey = stopped - placed adjacent to the service name, with NO accompanying status text or bordered badge. The primary action button reinforces it by flipping label and color (a neutral grey 'Start' becomes an active green/'Stop' state when the service is live). Herd adds lightweight per-site secured/linked glyphs rather than verbose status strings. The key move is that status is a pre-attentive color cue you perceive before reading, not a word you have to parse - which is exactly what lets a long list stay scannable. PortPilot can extend the binary dot into a 3-state cue (green = my dev app running, grey = my app stopped, faint/hollow = OS-system port noise) to encode signal-vs-noise in the same glance.
density_and_hierarchy: These apps handle 'many items' deliberately differently from a flat grid. (1) Row-not-card: a single-column list of hairline-separated rows is far denser and more scannable than a two-column grid of bordered cards, because the eye tracks one vertical line of focal points instead of zig-zagging a grid. (2) Rigid row anatomy: identity-glyph -> name+version -> port -> one toggle, always in the same x-positions, so the user reads columns, not boxes. (3) Grouping with collapsible section headers (Herd grouped sites + 'hide invalid' toggle): whole categories collapse to a line, so noise costs one row not N. (4) Master-detail: the row stays lean and verbose metadata lives in a detail pane shown only for the selected item - density without clutter. (5) Typographic hierarchy instead of borders: bold name, lighter muted version/port, so each row has internal structure without boxing. The combined effect is depth on three axes - status (color), grouping (sections), and detail (master-detail) - none of which PortPilot's current 33-equal-card wall has. DBngin admittedly only ever shows a handful of engines so it never needs virtualization; PortPilot with 33+ ports should pair this row model with grouping/collapse to keep the visible set small, and could virtualize if a scan ever returns hundreds.
caveats: Do not copy the menu-bar-ONLY footprint wholesale: Herd/DBngin are macOS menu-bar utilities where the window is secondary, but PortPilot is a full Electron app + VS Code sidebar + web portal, and its data density (33+ ports, full commands, PIDs) genuinely needs a primary window - treat the menu-bar idea as 'add a tray/status-bar quick-glance layer ON TOP of the window,' not 'demote the window.' Do not over-minimize: DBngin can be that sparse because it manages ~5 hand-created engines; PortPilot surfaces dozens of auto-discovered ports with real diagnostic metadata (command, PID, process), so stripping rows down to name+toggle would throw away information developers actually need - keep it in the detail panel, don't delete it. The single-green-accent palette is a starting hierarchy principle, not a theme mandate: PortPilot is explicitly multi-theme (TokyoNight, Dracula, Nord, etc.), so 'one semantic accent' must be expressed as a per-theme status token, not a hardcoded green. And DBngin's pure binary on/off is too coarse for PortPilot, which needs at least three states (my-running / my-stopped / OS-noise) plus possibly conflict/error - extend the dot vocabulary rather than adopting it verbatim.
applicability_reason: Herd and DBngin solve the exact same core shape as PortPilot - a list of local services you start/stop/inspect plus a settings surface - and their row-per-service + one-toggle + status-dot + grouped-sections + master-detail patterns map almost 1:1 onto PortPilot's active-ports, my-apps, status, and settings problems, with the only real gaps being scale (33+ auto-discovered items vs. a handful of hand-made ones) and platform footprint (menu-bar utility vs. full Electron/VS Code/web app).

tool: Raycast (command palette, List + Detail split, Settings/Preferences window)
one_liner: A keyboard-first launcher whose entire UI is one pattern repeated at every depth: a searchable, sectioned list of items with an icon on the left and accessory metadata on the right, optionally splitting into a List+Detail two-pane, governed by a context-aware action bar — and a settings window that is a two-pane sidebar-tab inspector, widely regarded as the gold standard for desktop preference UIs.

ui_patterns.pattern: Sectioned list with header titles + right-aligned count subtitles
ui_patterns.description: Raycast's root list is never a flat dump. Items are grouped into List.Section blocks, each with a small uppercase/muted header title on the left (e.g. 'Suggestions', 'Commands', 'Calculator') and frequently a count or subtitle right-aligned in the same header row. Within a section, rows are visually tight; between sections there's a header band that breaks the rhythm. The selected row gets a solid rounded highlight bar that spans the row width.
ui_patterns.why_not_flat: The header bands chunk a 40-item list into 4 scannable groups of ~10, so the eye lands on a category first and a row second. A flat list forces linear scanning; sections give a two-level read (group, then item) for free.

ui_patterns.pattern: Left icon + title + subtitle, with accessories pinned to the right edge
ui_patterns.description: Every row is a fixed three-zone layout: (1) a colored/app icon on the far left at a consistent size, (2) a primary title with an optional dimmer inline subtitle right after it, and (3) one or more 'accessories' right-aligned at the row's trailing edge. Accessories are small chips: a Tag (colored pill with transparent same-color background, e.g. a green 'Running' pill), plain colored text, a relative date ('1d', 'now'), or a tiny icon. Multiple accessories stack horizontally against the right margin.
ui_patterns.why_not_flat: The right-edge accessory rail turns each row into a mini data table: identity on the left, live status/metadata on the right, aligned across all rows so you can vertically scan just the status column. PortPilot's current cards bury PID/process in the middle of a box with no aligned status column — this pattern fixes exactly that.

ui_patterns.pattern: List + Detail two-pane split (isShowingDetail)
ui_patterns.description: Toggling detail mode collapses the list to a narrower left column (icon + title only, accessories hidden to save width) and reveals a right detail pane for the selected item. The detail pane has two stacked regions: a top markdown/free area, and a bottom structured Metadata block built from Label rows (title on the left, icon+value on the right), TagList rows (a wrap of colored tags), and Separator dividers. Selection in the left list instantly re-renders the right pane — no navigation, no modal.
ui_patterns.why_not_flat: This is master-detail done in-place: the list stays the navigator, the pane shows depth on demand. You get full detail (full command line, env, working dir, uptime) without a separate tab or popup. PortPilot today splits 'is it running / on what port' across two tabs; one List+Detail surface collapses that into one view.

ui_patterns.pattern: Context-aware bottom action bar (⌘K) instead of per-row buttons
ui_patterns.description: Rows carry almost no visible buttons. Instead the bottom bar shows the primary action label for the selected row (e.g. 'Open Command ↵') plus a single 'Actions ⌘K' affordance. Pressing ⌘K opens a small searchable action menu anchored bottom-right, listing every action available for that specific item with its keyboard shortcut on the right (Copy ⌘C, Kill ⌃X, Open in Browser ⌘O). Actions are contextual to the selected item's type.
ui_patterns.why_not_flat: It removes the per-card button clutter (PortPilot currently paints a copy icon + red X on all 33 cards) and replaces it with one quiet, discoverable menu. Hierarchy comes from hiding secondary actions behind ⌘K while keeping the one primary action always visible and labeled.

ui_patterns.pattern: Persistent fuzzy search bar as the primary navigation, not a filter afterthought
ui_patterns.description: The top of every Raycast surface is a single tall search input with a large placeholder. Typing fuzzy-filters the sectioned list live, and sections collapse/reorder by relevance as you type. It doubles as the command bar (type to filter, arrow to select, enter to act). The same input pattern recurs inside settings and inside the action menu.
ui_patterns.why_not_flat: Search is the depth mechanism for large lists: 33 ports become irrelevant once you type 'node' and see 2. It lets the default view stay grouped-and-calm while still giving instant random access, instead of a static filter box bolted onto a grid.

ui_patterns.pattern: Settings: two-pane window with a top icon-tab strip AND a left sub-sidebar
ui_patterns.description: The Settings window is a separate, fixed-size, non-modal window. Across the very top is a horizontal strip of large icon+label tabs (General, Extensions, AI, Cloud Sync, Account, Organizations, Advanced, About) — like a native macOS System Settings / Safari-prefs toolbar. Selecting a top tab swaps the entire body. For tabs with many items (Extensions, AI), the body itself is a two-pane: a searchable left sidebar listing every extension/command (with its icon), and a right form pane showing that item's preferences (token fields, dropdowns, hotkey recorders, enable toggles).
ui_patterns.why_not_flat: Three levels of hierarchy (top tab → sidebar item → form field) instead of PortPilot's single flat stack of bordered boxes. The top strip separates coarse domains; the left sidebar handles the long tail (one row per extension); the right pane stays focused on one thing. Nothing scrolls into an endless wall.

ui_patterns.pattern: Per-extension preference forms with typed, labeled, native controls and inline hotkey recorders
ui_patterns.description: In the Extensions tab, each extension's right pane is a tidy vertical form: label on the left, control on the right, with a small grey helper description under each control. Controls are typed — checkboxes for booleans, native dropdowns for enums, masked text fields for API tokens, and a 'record shortcut' button that captures a global hotkey live. Each command within an extension gets a row with an 'Alias' field and a hotkey recorder.
ui_patterns.why_not_flat: PortPilot's Settings is a flat stack of full-width bordered DATA/THEME/PREFERENCES boxes. Raycast's labeled-row form with typed controls + helper text is denser, more scannable, and reads as a real preferences inspector rather than a column of cards.

ui_patterns.pattern: Tag/pill vocabulary for status and type, with semantic color
ui_patterns.description: Raycast uses small rounded Tag pills with a transparent tinted background matching the text color (green = success/installed, yellow = update available, grey/blue = type labels). They appear both as list accessories and inside detail Metadata TagLists. Color is semantic and consistent, so a green pill always means the same thing regardless of where it shows up.
ui_patterns.why_not_flat: A consistent colored-pill status language lets the eye decode state pre-attentively (green dot = my server is up) without reading text. PortPilot has no status concept at all today; a single pill vocabulary (running/stopped/system/conflict) instantly separates signal from noise.

ui_patterns.pattern: Empty-width discipline and fixed compact density
ui_patterns.description: Raycast rows are a fixed, fairly tight height with generous but consistent horizontal padding, monochrome chrome, and exactly one accent color for selection. It never uses cards or boxes for list items — just rows with a hover/selected highlight. The window is a fixed modest size; content adapts via search and sections rather than sprawling.
ui_patterns.why_not_flat: Rows (not boxes) are inherently denser and more alignable than PortPilot's two-column card grid. Removing the per-item border/box chrome is itself a flatness fix — boxes shout 'every item is a separate equal thing', rows say 'these are entries in one list'.

steal_these.idea: Replace the two-column card grid with a sectioned row list grouped by meaning: 'My Dev Servers' (matched to registered apps), 'Other Local Servers', 'System / OS Ports'. Section headers carry a right-aligned count.
steal_these.how: Group the 33 ports into 3 List.Section-style bands. PortPilot already knows process names (node, svchost, System PID 4) — route well-known OS processes and ports <1024/system PIDs into a collapsed 'System' section so the user's :3000/:3001 sit alone at the top. The flat wall problem dies the moment grouping exists.

steal_these.idea: Adopt the left-icon + title + right-accessory-rail row layout with a semantic status pill as the first accessory.
steal_these.how: Each port becomes a row: framework/app icon on the left, ':3000 node' as title, truncated command as dim subtitle, and right-aligned accessories = a green 'running' pill + PID chip + a relative uptime ('2h'). Status becomes a scannable aligned column instead of being buried mid-card.

steal_these.idea: Merge MY APPS and ACTIVE PORTS into one List+Detail surface where a registered app and its live port are the same row.
steal_these.how: Use isShowingDetail-style split: left list = registered apps with a running/stopped pill accessory and the live port if up; selecting one opens a right detail pane showing the full command, working dir, env, live PID, uptime, and Start/Stop. This collapses the 'is my app running and on which port' question that's currently split across two disconnected tabs into a single answer.

steal_these.idea: Rebuild Settings as a two-pane sidebar-tab window: a left vertical nav (General, Appearance/Theme, Apps, Scanning, Data, About) with a focused right form pane per section.
steal_these.how: Drop the flat stack of full-width bordered boxes. Left sidebar items swap the right pane. Theme moves under 'Appearance' as a swatch grid; Auto-scan + interval under 'Scanning' as labeled rows with helper text; Export/Import under 'Data'. Three-level hierarchy replaces the one-level stack and it scales as settings grow.

steal_these.idea: Per-app preference forms in Raycast's labeled-row style with typed controls and an inline hotkey/alias recorder.
steal_these.how: In an 'Apps' settings pane, a searchable left list of registered apps; selecting one shows a right form: name, command (text), working dir (path), port (number), auto-start (toggle), plus a 'record global shortcut' button to start/stop that app from anywhere. Mirrors Raycast's per-extension preference pane exactly.

steal_these.idea: Add a context action bar with a ⌘K action menu instead of painting copy + kill buttons on every item.
steal_these.how: Show one primary action label for the selected row ('Open in Browser ↵') and an 'Actions ⌘K' affordance bottom-right. ⌘K opens a searchable menu of all actions for that port/app with shortcuts on the right (Copy command ⌘C, Kill ⌃X, Copy URL, Reveal process). Declutters all 33 rows at once.

steal_these.idea: Make the persistent fuzzy search bar the primary navigator across all surfaces, replacing the standalone filter input + count badge.
steal_these.how: One tall search input at the top of the unified ports/apps surface that fuzzy-filters live across port number, process, command, and app name. The '33 ports' count becomes a quiet right-aligned subtitle in the search row or the section headers, not a separate badge.

steal_these.idea: Define one semantic pill color vocabulary and reuse it everywhere (list accessory, detail metadata, VS Code tree, status bar).
steal_these.how: green = running, grey = stopped, blue = system/OS, amber = port conflict. Use the same tinted-transparent pill across the Electron list, the detail Metadata block, and as the basis for the VS Code 'PP: N running' counter and tree decorations, so status reads identically on every surface.

steal_these.idea: Convert the horizontal top-tab nav to a left rail (or icon strip) so it scales past 5 items and frees vertical space.
steal_these.how: ACTIVE PORTS | MY APPS | KNOWLEDGE | SETTINGS currently eats a horizontal band and won't grow. A slim left rail of icon+label items (Raycast-settings-style) reclaims vertical room for the list and leaves headroom for future sections (Logs, Groups) without re-flowing a top bar.

status_visualization: Raycast itself is mostly stateless, so its status language is borrowed from its building blocks rather than a live-process dashboard: the Tag accessory is the core device — a small rounded pill with text colored semantically and a transparent same-color background (green/yellow/grey). These appear right-aligned as list accessories and again inside List.Item.Detail.Metadata TagLists, so the same green pill means the same thing in both the row and the detail pane. Selection state is a single solid rounded highlight bar on the active row. There are no spinners or sparklines in the core UI; transient state is shown via a top-of-list 'loading' affordance and toast-style HUD confirmations after an action. For PortPilot the transferable kit is: (1) a semantic pill vocabulary (running/stopped/system/conflict) as the first right-rail accessory, (2) a relative-time accessory for uptime ('2h', '3d') using Raycast's auto-relative date formatting, and (3) a count subtitle in each section header (e.g. 'My Dev Servers — 2') so group-level status is visible before you scan rows. Notably Raycast does NOT use colored dots-per-row or live graphs, so don't over-import a 'monitoring dashboard' look; the pill + relative-time + section-count trio is enough to separate signal from noise.
density_and_hierarchy: Raycast handles large item counts through four stacked mechanisms rather than pagination or a scrollable wall. (1) Sections chunk the list into labeled groups so a 40-item list reads as 4 groups of ~10. (2) Persistent fuzzy search is the primary density tool — the default view stays grouped and calm, and typing collapses 40 items to the 2 that matter, with sections reordering by relevance. (3) The List+Detail split keeps each row minimal (icon + title only when detail is open) and pushes all per-item depth into the right pane on demand, so rows never bloat to carry their own detail. (4) Rows, not cards: a fixed compact row height with right-aligned aligned accessories makes the list read like a table you can vertically scan a single column of, which is far denser and more scannable than PortPilot's two-column box grid. Hierarchy is therefore three real levels deep everywhere — in the list (section → row → accessory) and in settings (top tab → sidebar item → form field) — versus PortPilot's current single flat level. The master-detail pattern is the key density lever for PortPilot: it lets the unified ports/apps list stay terse while still exposing full command lines, env, and uptime, solving both the 'flat wall' and the 'detail split across two tabs' problems at once.
caveats: Do not import Raycast's keyboard-only, mouse-hostile interaction model wholesale — PortPilot is a desktop utility many users will drive with a mouse, so the ⌘K action menu must have a visible mouse affordance (a '...' / kebab on row hover) and per-row primary actions can't be fully hidden behind shortcuts the way Raycast hides them. Don't copy Raycast's launcher chrome (the floating centered command window, the HUD, the 'press enter to run a command' framing); PortPilot is a persistent window app, not a launcher, so the list should be a stable panel, not a dismiss-on-blur overlay. The top icon-tab STRIP in Raycast settings is macOS-native-toolbar styling — recreate the structure (two-pane, sidebar items, focused form) but theme it to PortPilot's own design language rather than mimicking macOS chrome, especially since PortPilot must theme across 6 palettes and run on Windows. Avoid over-importing status visuals: Raycast deliberately has almost none, so resist turning the redesign into a metrics dashboard with graphs/dots — pills + relative-time + section counts is the right ceiling. Finally, fuzzy search is load-bearing in Raycast; if PortPilot adds sections but keeps a weak substring filter, it won't get the density payoff — the search has to actually fuzzy-match across port/process/command/app to make grouping pay off.
applicability_reason: PortPilot is almost exactly the shape Raycast is built for — a searchable list of start/stop/inspect-able items plus a preferences surface — and Raycast's sectioned-row-list, List+Detail split, semantic pill accessories, context action menu, and two-pane sidebar settings map one-to-one onto PortPilot's active-ports, my-apps, status, detail, and settings surfaces, directly dissolving the 'flat wall', 'no status', and 'detail split across two tabs' problems; the only friction is Raycast's launcher-overlay/keyboard-only chrome, which is structural and easily dropped.

tool: VS Code built-in Ports panel + Tree View API (TreeItem label/description/badge/contextValue, collapsible groups, viewsWelcome)
one_liner: VS Code's Ports view is a dense forwarded-port table (Port / Address / Running Process / Visibility / Origin) with hover-revealed inline icons, and its Tree View API gives extensions collapsible groups, dimmed description text, theme-colored status icons, hover inline actions, numeric view badges, and welcome-view buttons - exactly the hierarchy/status vocabulary PortPilot's flat grid lacks.

ui_patterns.pattern: Multi-column port table with named columns (Port / Forwarded Address / Running Process / Visibility / Origin)
ui_patterns.description: The Ports view is a TABLE, not a grid of cards. Each row is one port with aligned columns: the local port number, the forwarded/localhost address (clickable), the Running Process column showing the actual command/binary that owns the port, a Visibility pill (Private/Public), and an Origin column (User Forwarded / Auto Forwarded / Static). Columns are scannable top-to-bottom: your eye runs down the Process column to find 'node', down the Port column to find ':3000'.
ui_patterns.why_not_flat: A table aligns the SAME attribute across every row, so the user scans one dimension (process, or port, or visibility) instead of re-reading 33 self-contained boxes. PortPilot's two-column card grid forces a full re-read of each card because PROCESS/PID/COMMAND live in different positions visually within each card. Columns kill that.

ui_patterns.pattern: Hover-revealed inline action icons (group: "inline")
ui_patterns.description: A port row shows NO buttons at rest - just data. On row hover, a cluster of icon-buttons fades in on the right edge: copy-address, open-in-browser, open-in-preview, stop-forwarding, set-visibility. The row stays calm and data-dense until you reach for it. Actions are right-aligned and consistent across every row so muscle memory works.
ui_patterns.why_not_flat: PortPilot currently paints a copy-icon AND a red kill-X on every one of 33 cards permanently, so 66 always-visible buttons compete with the data and amplify the wall-of-boxes feeling. Hover-reveal removes that constant chrome, letting the data itself create the visual rhythm; controls appear only on the row you're targeting.

ui_patterns.pattern: Collapsible grouped tree (TreeItemCollapsibleState.Collapsed/Expanded) with a parent header row
ui_patterns.description: Tree View extensions render top-level group nodes (a label + twistie/chevron) that expand to reveal children indented one level. A group header can itself carry a description and an icon. Groups can default-collapsed so noise stays folded away and default-expanded for the section you care about. The chevron + indentation creates an obvious two-level depth.
ui_patterns.why_not_flat: This is the single biggest fix for PortPilot's flatness: instead of 33 equal boxes, you get 'MY DEV SERVERS (2)' expanded at top and 'SYSTEM / OS PORTS (28)' collapsed below. Hierarchy and signal-vs-noise separation come for free from the indent + twistie, with zero new visual language to invent.

ui_patterns.pattern: Label + dimmed description on one line (TreeItem.label vs TreeItem.description)
ui_patterns.description: Each tree row has a bright primary label and, on the SAME line after it, a dimmed/muted secondary 'description' string. VS Code uses this everywhere: filename (label) + git status or line-count (description); extension name + version. The eye reads the bright token first, the grey metadata second, without a second line of height.
ui_patterns.why_not_flat: PortPilot stacks PORT (huge), then PROCESS, then PID, then COMMAND as equal-weight stacked lines, making every card tall and visually identical. Collapsing to 'node :3000' (label) + 'PID 18244 - next dev' (dimmed description) on one line creates intra-row hierarchy and halves card height, so more fits on screen without a wall.

ui_patterns.pattern: ThemeIcon with theme color as a status glyph (e.g. iconPath = new ThemeIcon('circle-filled', new ThemeColor('charts.green')))
ui_patterns.description: Tree rows lead with a small icon whose COLOR carries meaning pulled from the active theme palette: a green filled circle = running, grey = stopped, red/orange = error/conflict. Because the color is a ThemeColor token, it auto-adapts to every theme (TokyoNight, Nord, Dracula) instead of being hard-coded. The icon sits left of the label as a persistent at-a-glance status read.
ui_patterns.why_not_flat: PortPilot has NO status concept at all right now - a port is just there or not. A leading colored status dot introduces a status dimension cheaply and, crucially, themes itself across PortPilot's 6 swatches via the same ThemeColor pattern, so it works in Brutalist Light and Dracula without per-theme art.

ui_patterns.pattern: Numeric badge on the view title (TreeView.badge / 'PP: N running' style status-bar item)
ui_patterns.description: The Ports/Apps view title carries a small numeric badge (count of items), and VS Code surfaces an aggregate count in the status bar. PortPilot's extension already does the status-bar 'PP: N running' counter - the badge is the same idea promoted to the view header and to group headers ('SYSTEM PORTS (28)').
ui_patterns.why_not_flat: A count badge per group turns the header into a summary line, so a collapsed group still tells you 'there are 28 OS ports in here' without expanding. The current '33 ports' count badge is a single flat total; splitting it into per-group badges communicates structure at a glance.

ui_patterns.pattern: viewsWelcome empty-state with a link-as-button
ui_patterns.description: When a tree view has no items, VS Code shows centered welcome markdown where a link alone on its own line renders as a full-width button (e.g. 'You have no forwarded ports.' + a [Forward a Port] button). It turns an empty void into a guided primary action.
ui_patterns.why_not_flat: Gives PortPilot's MY APPS (when no projects registered) and a filtered-to-empty Active Ports a real onboarding affordance - a single obvious [Add App] / [Scan Ports] button - instead of a blank panel, reinforcing that the surface is alive and actionable.

ui_patterns.pattern: Right-click context menu layered over inline actions (menu groups: inline vs navigation vs 1_modification), contextValue-gated
ui_patterns.description: The same row exposes 2-3 high-frequency actions as inline hover icons AND a fuller set on right-click, with menu items gated by contextValue (e.g. a kill action only appears on rows whose contextValue == 'killablePort', not on protected System ports). Groups order the menu: 'inline' for hover icons, 'navigation' top section, named groups below.
ui_patterns.why_not_flat: Lets PortPilot show only safe actions inline (copy, open) and bury or DISABLE 'kill' on OS/system ports (:135 svchost, :445 System PID 4) via a contextValue gate, instead of rendering an identical red kill-X on a System-owned port the user should never kill. That's both safer and a real visual differentiator between 'my' rows and 'system' rows.

steal_these.idea: Replace the uniform two-column card grid with a collapsible grouped tree/table: 'MY DEV SERVERS' (expanded) over 'SYSTEM / OS PORTS' (collapsed), each header carrying a count badge.
steal_these.how: Group the ~33 scanned ports by classifying owner: known dev processes (node, vite, python, next, the user's registered apps) go in the expanded top group; svchost/System/PID 4 and well-known OS ports go in a collapsed 'System' group. Headers read 'MY DEV SERVERS (2)' / 'SYSTEM PORTS (28)'. This alone converts the wall of equal boxes into signal-over-noise hierarchy.

steal_these.idea: Switch each port from a stacked card to a single dense row: leading colored status dot, bright label ('node :3000'), dimmed description ('PID 18244 - next dev - C:/Scratch/...'), hover-revealed inline icons.
steal_these.how: Adopt label-vs-description: primary token bright, metadata dimmed on the same line. Move copy/open/kill into a hover-revealed right-aligned icon cluster (group:inline) instead of always-on buttons. Halves row height, adds intra-row hierarchy, and removes 66 always-visible buttons of chrome.

steal_these.idea: Introduce a ThemeColor-driven status glyph as the universal status vocabulary across all three surfaces.
steal_these.how: Green filled circle = running, grey = stopped/idle, amber = port conflict, red = error. Drive the color from a CSS variable per theme (mirroring VS Code ThemeColor) so it survives all 6 PortPilot themes. Reuse the exact same glyph in the desktop rows, the VS Code tree, and the web portal so status reads identically everywhere.

steal_these.idea: Merge MY APPS and ACTIVE PORTS into one correlated view by showing each registered app's LIVE port and running state inline, the way the Ports table shows Running Process.
steal_these.how: Each registered app row gets the same status dot + 'running on :3001' dimmed description when its process is detected in the port scan. The 'is my app running and on which port' question is answered in one row instead of mentally joining two disconnected tabs. Keep start/stop as hover-inline actions on the same row.

steal_these.idea: Gate destructive actions by a contextValue equivalent so OS/system ports cannot be killed (or show kill disabled), differentiating row types visually and safely.
steal_these.how: Tag each port row with an owner-class ('dev' | 'system' | 'registered'). 'system' rows hide/disable the kill control and render with a muted treatment; 'dev' and 'registered' rows get the full inline action set. This both prevents footguns (killing :445 System) and makes the two row classes look meaningfully different rather than identical.

steal_these.idea: Add a per-group count badge and a viewsWelcome-style empty state with a single primary button.
steal_these.how: Promote the flat '33 ports' total into per-group badges on each collapsible header. For empty states (no registered apps, or filter matches nothing), show a centered message plus one link-as-button ([Add App] / [Scan Ports]) instead of a blank panel.

status_visualization: VS Code's primary status mechanism is a leading ThemeIcon whose COLOR is a semantic ThemeColor token (green 'circle-filled' = running, grey = stopped, red/orange = error), rendered left of the label so status is read before identity. It is reinforced by (a) numeric badges on the view title and group headers for counts, (b) the status-bar aggregate counter (PortPilot already ships 'PP: N running'), and (c) the Visibility pill (Private/Public) in the Ports table which is itself a small colored state token. Critically the status comes from a theme palette token, not hard-coded hex, so it adapts across themes - exactly what PortPilot needs given its 6 swatches. PortPilot currently has NO status dimension on Active Ports; adopting the colored-dot-driven-by-CSS-variable pattern is the cheapest high-impact win.
density_and_hierarchy: VS Code handles many items via three stacked techniques rather than a flat list. (1) Collapsible groups (TreeItemCollapsibleState) fold noise away - a default-collapsed 'System' group hides 28 OS ports behind one header line while keeping the count visible via a badge, so density is on-demand. (2) The table layout aligns one attribute per column so scanning is one-dimensional (run down the Process column) instead of re-reading whole cards. (3) The label/description split puts identity (bright) and metadata (dimmed) on a single line, so each item is one row tall, not a four-line card - dramatically more items per screen. Indentation under group headers supplies the depth cue. The result scales to hundreds of items (VS Code's own Explorer, Source Control, Ports all do this) where PortPilot's equal-weight card grid visibly breaks down at 33. Progressive disclosure (collapsed groups + hover-only actions + right-click for the long tail) keeps the resting state calm and the detail one interaction away.
caveats: Do not literally clone VS Code's chrome - PortPilot is a standalone Electron app with its own per-project aesthetic (per Macdara's rules, no inherited default look), so steal the STRUCTURE (groups, columns, label/description, status dot, hover actions) not the grey VS Code skin. The Tree View API specifics (contextValue when-clauses, group:inline menu contributions, viewsWelcome markdown) apply ONLY to PortPilot's actual VS Code extension surface; the desktop renderer (vanilla HTML/CSS/JS) must re-implement the same patterns by hand in CSS/JS, not via the API. A real tree with twisties can feel heavy for only TWO groups - if there are just 'mine' vs 'system', consider a simple section header + collapse toggle rather than a full recursive tree widget; don't over-engineer infinite nesting PortPilot will never use. VS Code's port TABLE wants horizontal width - on the narrow VS Code sidebar VS Code itself drops to a tree, so PortPilot's desktop (wide) can be a table but the extension sidebar should stay a label/description tree. Finally, the right-click context menu is a VS Code-native affordance; replicating a full context menu in the Electron renderer is extra work - hover-inline actions cover 90% of the value, so prioritize those over a custom context-menu system.
applicability_reason: This is the closest possible reference - PortPilot literally has a VS Code extension surface that already uses two Tree Views and a status-bar counter, and VS Code's own Ports panel solves the identical problem (a dense list of ports/processes you start/stop/inspect with status and grouping), so nearly every pattern maps one-to-one onto all three PortPilot surfaces.

tool: TablePlus (DB client) + Postman/Insomnia (API clients) — "sidebar of saved things + tabbed master-detail" pattern
one_liner: Database and API clients that manage hundreds of saved connections/requests via a grouped, color-coded, collapsible left sidebar feeding a tabbed master-detail content pane — the exact "list of items you start/inspect plus settings" shape PortPilot needs.

ui_patterns.pattern: Collapsible grouped sidebar with disclosure triangles (folders/groups)
ui_patterns.description: TablePlus's welcome screen and Postman/Insomnia sidebars render saved items inside named, collapsible containers. TablePlus connection 'Groups' are created via right-click 'New group' with a name + icon, and connections are dragged into them; the group is a collapsible header row. Postman/Insomnia nest Collection > Folder > Subfolder > Request, each level a triangle you expand/collapse. The default state can be all-collapsed so you see ~6 group headers instead of 200 rows.
ui_patterns.why_not_flat: A single triangle row stands in for N children, so the eye scans group headers first (depth level 1) and only drills into the one relevant group. The wall of equal rows becomes a short index of categories that expand on demand — progressive disclosure instead of a flat dump.

ui_patterns.pattern: Per-item status/environment COLOR as the primary visual key
ui_patterns.description: TablePlus assigns every connection a 'status color' (set in the connection form, e.g. red=production, yellow=staging, green=local) rendered as a colored dot/stripe on the sidebar row AND as a tint on the active window's title bar so you always know which DB you're touching. Insomnia color-codes sub-environments via a colored icon. The color is a deliberate signal of environment/risk, not decoration.
ui_patterns.why_not_flat: Color is a pre-attentive channel — you locate 'the red one' before reading any text. In a flat monochrome list every row competes equally for attention; a color key lets a 33-item list resolve to 'the 3 green dev ones' instantly without sorting or filtering.

ui_patterns.pattern: HTTP-method / type badge as a fixed-width colored prefix on every row
ui_patterns.description: Postman and Insomnia prefix each request row with a short, color-coded method chip: GET in green, POST in orange/yellow, PUT in blue, DELETE in red, etc., left-aligned in a fixed column so they form a scannable vertical ribbon. The label text follows. The badge encodes the item's KIND in a glanceable token.
ui_patterns.why_not_flat: A fixed-position colored token column turns a list into a typed table — you read down the badge column to find 'all the POSTs' without reading names. PortPilot's ports have an analogous 'kind' axis (system/OS vs user dev server) crying out for exactly this treatment.

ui_patterns.pattern: Master-detail: sidebar selection drives a rich right-hand detail pane
ui_patterns.description: Selecting a connection (TablePlus) or request (Postman/Insomnia) doesn't navigate away — it loads a detail surface on the right: TablePlus shows the table list + data grid + a right sidebar of structure/columns/indexes; Postman shows the request builder with sub-tabs (Params, Headers, Body, Tests, Pre-request, Settings). The list stays visible and persistent on the left.
ui_patterns.why_not_flat: Two-pane master-detail replaces PortPilot's tab-switching (Active Ports tab vs My Apps tab) with one persistent context. You never lose your place in the list to see an item's details, and the detail pane can be arbitrarily deep without bloating the list rows.

ui_patterns.pattern: Tabbed content area with pinned/temporary (italic) tabs
ui_patterns.description: Postman and TablePlus open each opened item as a tab across the top of the content pane. Postman uses a 'preview tab' convention (single-click = temporary italic tab that gets replaced by the next single-click; double-click or edit = pinned permanent tab). Tabs are reorderable by drag, closable with a middle-click or x, and overflow into a chevron dropdown.
ui_patterns.why_not_flat: Tabs let the user keep 4-5 active items 'open' simultaneously and flip between them — a working set distinct from the full saved list. The preview-tab trick prevents tab-clutter from casual browsing. For PortPilot this models 'the apps I'm actively babysitting right now' vs 'everything registered'.

ui_patterns.pattern: Pinned/favourited items float to a sticky top section
ui_patterns.description: Insomnia lets you pin requests so they surface in a 'Pinned' band at the top of the collection, above the normal tree (the GitHub issue #6427 confirms pinning is a first-class sidebar concept). Postman stars/favourites collections. TablePlus keeps recent/important connections near the top of the welcome list.
ui_patterns.why_not_flat: A sticky 'pinned' band creates a two-tier hierarchy within one list: the 3-5 things you touch daily live at the top regardless of alphabetical/scan order, and the long tail sits below. This directly answers 'separate my real dev servers from the noise.'

ui_patterns.pattern: Persistent sidebar filter/search box pinned above the tree
