ui_patterns.description: All three put a single filter input at the top of the sidebar that does live substring filtering across the whole tree, collapsing non-matching groups and highlighting matches. Postman's sidebar filter, Insomnia's collection filter, TablePlus's connection search all behave this way — type-to-narrow without leaving the keyboard.
ui_patterns.why_not_flat: Filter + grouping compose: the structure gives you browse-ability, the filter gives you jump-to. A flat list with no filter forces linear scanning; the combination means even a 200-item tree is navigable in two keystrokes.

ui_patterns.pattern: Right-click context menu carries the per-item verbs (not inline buttons on every row)
ui_patterns.description: TablePlus connections, Postman requests, and Insomnia folders all expose their actions (Edit, Duplicate, Color, New group, Delete, Move) via right-click context menu rather than a row crowded with buttons. The row itself stays clean — just icon, color, name — and hover reveals at most a single overflow ('...') affordance.
ui_patterns.why_not_flat: Moving verbs off the row into a context menu (or single hover-revealed kebab) lets each row be dense and quiet. PortPilot's cards currently carry a copy button + red X on every one of 33 cards, which is visually noisy; deferring actions to hover/right-click makes the list scannable as data first, actionable second.

steal_these.idea: Replace the flat 33-card grid with a collapsible grouped LIST: 'My Dev Servers', 'Known Tools (Docker/Vite/etc.)', 'System / OS Ports' as three group headers, system ports collapsed by default
steal_these.how: Classify each scanned port by process name + PID (PID 4 / svchost / System = OS group; ports matching a registered app = dev group; everything else = other). Render TablePlus-style collapsible group headers with a count badge each ('My Dev Servers 4', 'System 19'). System group ships collapsed so the signal sits at the top and the OS noise is one click away, not in your face.

steal_these.idea: Add a per-port/per-app status color dot as the leftmost element of every row
steal_these.how: Borrow TablePlus's status-color idea: green dot = my app running healthy, gold/amber = registered-but-stopped, red = port conflict / killable, grey = system-owned. The dot is the pre-attentive key so 'which of my servers is up' resolves before reading any text — far stronger than today's uniform blue ':PORT' typography.

steal_these.idea: Merge Active Ports + My Apps into ONE master-detail surface with a persistent left sidebar and a tabbed detail pane
steal_these.how: Kill the Active Ports / My Apps tab split. Left sidebar = grouped tree of apps and live ports (a running registered app shows its live port inline as a child/badge). Click an item → right-hand detail pane (Postman master-detail) shows process, PID, full command, uptime, logs, and start/stop/kill controls. 'Is my app running and on what port' becomes one glance, not two tabs.

steal_these.idea: Adopt a type/kind BADGE column like Postman's GET/POST chips
steal_these.how: Give each port row a fixed-width colored kind chip: 'DEV' (blue), 'SYS' (grey), 'DB' (purple for :5432/:3306), 'WEB' (green for :80/:443/:3000). The chip column forms a scannable ribbon so the user reads down it to find their dev servers without reading process names — the typed-table effect that breaks the flat wall.

steal_these.idea: Pin/favourite the apps you babysit daily into a sticky top band
steal_these.how: Insomnia-style pinning: a star/pin toggle (already exposed via the toggle_favorite MCP tool) floats chosen apps into a 'Pinned' band at the top of the sidebar above the grouped tree, so the 3-4 projects you run every day are always at row 1-4 regardless of how many ports are live.

steal_these.idea: Move per-row actions to hover-reveal + right-click; replace tabs nav with a settings sub-sidebar
steal_these.how: Stop rendering copy + red-X on all 33 cards; show a single hover kebab/overflow and a right-click menu (Copy command, Open in browser, Kill, Add as app). For SETTINGS, replace the flat stack of bordered boxes with a TablePlus-preferences-style two-pane: a small left sub-nav (Theme / Preferences / Data / Knowledge) driving a detail pane on the right — same master-detail grammar as the main view, so navigation feels consistent and scales past 5 sections without the top-tab ceiling.

status_visualization: TablePlus is the gold standard here: a deliberate per-connection STATUS COLOR (red=prod, amber=staging, green=local) that appears both as a sidebar dot and as a tint on the active window chrome, so environment/risk is encoded in a pre-attentive channel rather than text. Postman/Insomnia encode item KIND via fixed-position color chips (GET green, POST orange, DELETE red) forming a scannable badge ribbon, plus a small live request-running spinner during execution. None of them use a uniform monochrome treatment — color always carries either environment-risk or item-type meaning. For PortPilot the lift is a two-channel scheme: a colored status DOT for run-state (green up / amber stopped / red conflict / grey system) and a colored KIND chip (DEV/SYS/DB/WEB), which together let a 33-item list resolve visually in under a second versus today's wall of identical blue ':PORT' boxes.
density_and_hierarchy: These tools routinely hold hundreds of saved items and stay navigable via four composing mechanisms, none of which PortPilot currently uses: (1) collapsible named GROUPS/folders so N items collapse to one header row with a count badge — the primary defense against a flat wall; (2) a sticky PINNED/favourites band that lifts the daily-driver items above the long tail; (3) a persistent type-to-filter box at the top of the sidebar for jump-to-by-name without leaving the keyboard; and (4) MASTER-DETAIL so each row stays terse (color dot + kind chip + name) while arbitrary depth lives in the right-hand detail pane and tabs, never bloating the list. Postman's preview-tab (italic temporary tab replaced on next single-click) further controls clutter so casual browsing doesn't spawn 30 tabs. The lesson for PortPilot: rows should be DENSE and QUIET (one line, two color tokens, name) and all richness — command, PID, logs, actions — moves into the detail pane and context menu, so 33 ports read as a short grouped index, not a grid of paragraphs.
caveats: Do NOT copy the full DB/API-client weight. PortPilot has a fixed, machine-bounded set (~33 ports, a handful of apps), so heavyweight collection/folder hierarchies, nested subfolders, multi-workspace switchers, and per-item environment variables are over-engineering — one flat level of 3-4 auto-classified groups is enough; do not give users manual folder management. Postman's preview-tab convention is subtle and confuses new users; only adopt tabs if PortPilot genuinely needs multiple items open at once (it may not — a single detail pane could suffice). TablePlus's manual per-connection color assignment is good for DBs where the user knows prod vs staging, but PortPilot should DERIVE status color automatically from run-state/process, not ask the user to set it. Avoid Postman's notorious sidebar density/cramping and its over-deep right-click menus — PortPilot's verb set is tiny (start/stop/kill/open/copy), so keep menus to 4-5 items. And resist importing the API-client visual language (request-builder sub-tabs like Params/Headers/Body) literally; borrow the master-detail STRUCTURE, not the form fields.
applicability_reason: The 'grouped color-coded sidebar of saved things feeding a tabbed master-detail pane' is almost a one-to-one structural match for PortPilot's apps+ports+settings, and the four anti-flatness mechanisms (grouping, status color, pinning, master-detail) directly solve the brief's stated problems of flatness, no grouping, no status, and the apps/ports tab split.

tool: Tailscale (macOS menu-bar popover + windowed app v1.88+) and Mullvad VPN desktop app
one_liner: Two consumer "list of things with on/off state" apps where a tiny tray popover is the primary surface: Tailscale shows a sectioned, status-dotted device list with a master/detail windowed mode; Mullvad shows one giant connect button over a hierarchical country-city-server location tree.

ui_patterns.pattern: Sectioned tray popover with a pinned 'This Device' header card
ui_patterns.description: Tailscale's menu-bar dropdown does not open as a flat list. The top is a fixed self-card: your own machine name, its 100.x Tailscale IP, and a connection-health line, visually separated (heavier weight, a divider rule) from the scrollable 'Devices' / 'Exit nodes' sections below it. The one row you always care about (am I connected, what's my address) is lifted out of the list entirely and pinned at the top.
ui_patterns.why_not_flat: It establishes a primary/secondary hierarchy before the list even starts - the user's own status is a header, peers are body. A flat list would force the self-row to compete visually with 40 peer rows.

ui_patterns.pattern: Per-row colored status dot as the leftmost glyph
ui_patterns.description: Every Tailscale device row leads with a small filled circle: green/solid = online and directly reachable, grey/hollow = offline, amber/yellow = relayed or degraded (DERP relay instead of direct). The dot sits in a fixed left gutter so all dots align into a single scannable vertical column; the eye reads the column of colors, not 30 individual rows.
ui_patterns.why_not_flat: Color-coded state in a fixed gutter turns a list into a status board. You triage by glancing down one column of dots instead of reading text in every row - signal (online things) visually separates from noise (offline things) with zero sorting.

ui_patterns.pattern: One dominant primary action vs. a quiet secondary list (Mullvad)
ui_patterns.description: Mullvad's whole window is dominated by a single large pill button that is GREEN labelled 'Secure my connection' when disconnected and turns RED 'Disconnect' when connected, with a colored 'connecting…/blocked' transitional state and a map/shield that shifts color with status. The location picker is a smaller 'Switch location' affordance below it. There is exactly one obvious thing to do; everything else is subordinate.
ui_patterns.why_not_flat: Instead of N equal controls, there is a strict size/color hierarchy: one hero action, then a list. The button IS the status indicator (its color and label encode the connection state), collapsing 'show me state' and 'change state' into one glanceable element.

ui_patterns.pattern: Disclosure-triangle hierarchy: country → city → server (Mullvad)
ui_patterns.description: Mullvad's location list is a collapsible tree, not a flat roster of hundreds of servers. You see countries; an expand chevron on the right opens cities; cities expand to individual servers. A green dot marks where you're currently connected, and the currently-selected branch auto-expands. Hundreds of endpoints collapse to a dozen visible country rows.
ui_patterns.why_not_flat: Progressive disclosure: density is hidden behind expansion. The default view is a short scannable list of countries; detail is one click deep, so the surface never becomes a wall of 600 server rows.

ui_patterns.pattern: Master-detail windowed mode as the 'full' counterpart to the popover
ui_patterns.description: Tailscale v1.88+ added a real resizable window alongside the tray: left = searchable device/exit-node list with status, right = detail panel for the selected device (copyable Tailscale IP, copyable MagicDNS name, status, and action buttons - Ping, Taildrop send). Same data as the popover, but the list stays visible while you inspect one item.
ui_patterns.why_not_flat: Two-pane master/detail means selecting an item enriches a side panel instead of pushing you to a separate screen - inspection and the list coexist. Depth (per-item detail) is added without a navigation jump or a second disconnected tab.

ui_patterns.pattern: Inline per-row hover actions instead of a context menu
ui_patterns.description: In Tailscale rows the row is the affordance: hovering reveals 'Copy IP' / connect-as-exit-node controls inline; clicking the row name often copies the address. Mullvad rows reveal a connect action on the row itself. Actions live where the item lives, not behind a right-click or a separate toolbar.
ui_patterns.why_not_flat: Actions attached to each row give the list a second layer of interaction without adding visible chrome - the list looks calm at rest but is action-dense on hover, so it reads as a clean list yet behaves like a control panel.

ui_patterns.pattern: Latency / metric annotation on exit-node and server rows
ui_patterns.description: Tailscale's new exit-node selector and Mullvad's relay list annotate rows with a secondary metric - latency / ping, or 'suggested' badges based on location/latency. The metric is right-aligned and dimmer than the name, so it reads as a sortable secondary attribute, not a competing label.
ui_patterns.why_not_flat: A right-aligned dim metric column adds a quantitative dimension to each row (good vs. bad choice) without bolding it into noise - the row now carries name + state + quality in one line via typographic weight hierarchy.

ui_patterns.pattern: Search-to-filter a long list instead of paginating it
ui_patterns.description: Both windowed Tailscale and Mullvad put a search/filter field at the top of the list; typing narrows the device or location list live. This is the primary navigation for large tailnets/server fleets rather than scrolling.
ui_patterns.why_not_flat: Filtering converts a long flat list into a short relevant one on demand - the user never confronts all 33/300 items at once, they type to collapse it to the handful that matter.

ui_patterns.pattern: Dock/tray icon as ambient status, red-dot for errors
ui_patterns.description: Tailscale shows connection state on the menu-bar icon itself and overlays a 'very visible red dot' on the dock icon during critical errors; Mullvad's tray icon color reflects secured/unsecured. The smallest possible surface (a 16px icon) carries the single most important bit.
ui_patterns.why_not_flat: State is legible before any window opens - the persistent surface is itself a status indicator, so the full UI is only needed for changes, not for the constant 'is it working?' check.

steal_these.idea: Pin a 'This Machine' header card above Active Ports - your dev box's hostname, count of YOUR running dev servers, and overall 'N apps up' health - visually separated from the port list below.
steal_these.how: Mirror Tailscale's pinned self-card. PortPilot's top of ACTIVE PORTS becomes a header strip ('3 dev servers running, 30 system ports') instead of starting cold into the 33-card grid; the thing you care about is lifted out of the wall.

steal_these.idea: Lead every port/app row with a colored status dot in a fixed left gutter: green=your running dev server, grey=system/OS port, amber=conflict/unexpected-process-on-expected-port.
steal_these.how: Replace the uniform blue ':PORT' cards with rows that align a status dot column. The OS noise (:135, :139, :445) becomes a grey block the eye skips; your :3000/:3001 node servers glow green at the top of the scan - solving the flatness directly with one glyph column.

steal_these.idea: Group the flat port grid into collapsible sections - 'My Dev Servers' (expanded), 'Other User Apps', 'System / OS Ports' (collapsed by default) - like Mullvad's country→city tree.
steal_these.how: Use disclosure triangles. svchost/System ports collapse into one folded 'System (28)' row; the default view is a dozen rows of real signal. Density is hidden behind expansion instead of dumped into a 33-box wall.

steal_these.idea: Adopt a master-detail layout: left = the port/app list, right = detail panel for the selected entry (full command, PID, working dir, copyable URL, Kill / Open / Restart buttons).
steal_these.how: Copy Tailscale's windowed two-pane. The truncated COMMAND line and copy/kill buttons move OUT of every card into a right-hand inspector that populates on row-click - the grid gets calmer, detail gets richer, and inspection no longer needs a separate tab.

steal_these.idea: Merge MY APPS and ACTIVE PORTS into one unified list keyed on the app, where a registered app shows its live status dot + actual bound port inline - the way a Tailscale row shows a device and its live reachability together.
steal_these.how: A registered app row reads 'BloodClarity ● running :3000' with a Stop button, or 'BloodClarity ○ stopped' with Start. Unregistered live ports list below under 'Untracked'. Kills the split-brain where 'is my app running and on what port' spans two disconnected tabs.

steal_these.idea: Build a tray-mode popover whose top is a single hero status line + primary action, exactly like Mullvad's one-button window, then the dev-server list below.
steal_these.how: PortPilot tray dropdown: header '3 servers running' (green) / 'all stopped' (grey), one-tap toggle per app inline, click-row-to-open-in-browser. The menu-bar icon shows the running count (reuse the existing 'PP: N running' concept) so state is ambient without opening anything.

steal_these.idea: Replace the horizontal top-tabs (won't scale past ~5) with a left vertical nav rail; in tray/compact mode collapse settings behind a gear, and use search-to-filter as the primary way through a 33-item list.
steal_these.how: Tailscale/Mullvad never use horizontal tabs - a vertical rail or sectioned popover scales. Add a live filter box at the top of Active Ports so the user types ':300' to collapse 33 ports to the 2 that matter, instead of scanning the grid.

status_visualization: Both apps make state glanceable through three layers: (1) the persistent tray/dock icon itself encodes the top-level bit (Tailscale icon shows connected/not; Mullvad tray icon color = secured/unsecured; a red dot overlays the dock icon on critical error). (2) Per-row colored status dots in a fixed left gutter - Tailscale: green=online+direct, amber/yellow=relayed/degraded, grey/hollow=offline - so a column of dots is read instead of rows of text. (3) The hero control doubles as a status display - Mullvad's big button is green 'Secure my connection' when off, red 'Disconnect' when on, with distinct transitional 'connecting/blocked' colors, so the same element shows state AND changes it. Secondary metrics (latency, 'suggested') are right-aligned and dimmed so quality reads without competing with the name. For PortPilot this maps cleanly: a green/grey/amber dot per port (mine/system/conflict), a tray icon carrying the running count, and a header line summarizing 'N dev servers up'.
density_and_hierarchy: Tailscale handles many peers via: a pinned self-card (primary lifted out of the list), sectioning (Devices vs. Exit nodes), search-to-filter as primary navigation on big tailnets, a status-dot gutter so the list scans by color not text, and a master-detail window where per-device depth lives in a right panel rather than inflating every row. Mullvad handles hundreds of servers via a strict country→city→server disclosure tree - the default view is a dozen country rows, with cities/servers one expansion deep and the active branch auto-expanded - plus a single dominant action so the eye has one anchor. Neither ever shows a uniform wall: density is always either collapsed behind disclosure, filtered by search, or demoted to a detail pane. The directly transferable moves for PortPilot's 33-box grid: collapse system/OS ports into one folded section, pin a summary header, add a filter box, push the COMMAND/PID detail into a right inspector, and use a dot gutter to separate signal from noise without sorting.
caveats: Do not copy the single-hero-button pattern literally - Mullvad has ONE binary action (connect/disconnect) because it has one tunnel; PortPilot manages N independent apps, so a per-row toggle (Tailscale's model) fits, not one giant button. The hero element should be a status summary, not a single control. Avoid over-applying the popover-as-primary idea to the desktop Electron app: tray mode is a great ADDITION but the full window is where multi-port/multi-app management belongs (Tailscale itself added a windowed mode precisely because the popover hid power features). Don't mimic Mullvad's deep 3-level tree for ports - port lists are shallow (one level: app→port), so 2 levels of grouping (section→row) is plenty; a 3-deep tree would be ceremony. Tailscale's 'relayed/amber' nuance has no clean port-manager analog - don't invent a third state just to have one; green=mine / grey=system, plus amber reserved only for genuine port conflicts, is the honest mapping. Finally, both apps are dark-minimal with restrained color; PortPilot's existing 6-theme system means the status-dot palette must be defined per-theme via CSS variables, not hardcoded.
applicability_reason: PortPilot's core failure - a flat wall of equal items with no status, grouping, or signal/noise separation, plus a desire for a tray mode - is almost exactly the problem these two apps already solved with status-dot gutters, pinned self-cards, collapsible grouping, master-detail panels, and tray-popover-as-primary, making them a near-perfect structural template.

tool: Process monitors: btop/btm (TUI), htop, macOS Activity Monitor, Windows 11 Task Manager
one_liner: Real-time system/process monitors that turn hundreds of equal-weight rows into a scannable, sortable, color-graded hierarchy using dense tables, tree grouping, inline sparklines, heat-shaded cells, and a persistent select-row-to-detail panel.

ui_patterns.pattern: Dense sortable column table with a sticky highlighted sort header
ui_patterns.description: btop, htop, Activity Monitor and Task Manager all render processes as a real table: fixed columns (PID, NAME/COMMAND, USER, CPU%, MEM, PORT-equivalent) with a header row. Clicking a header (or pressing 's' in btop/btm) sorts by that column and marks the active column - btop brightens the sorted column's header and draws a little up/down arrow; Activity Monitor shades the active sort header blue with a triangle. One click flips ascending/descending. The default and most-used sort is CPU%-descending, so the heaviest thing is always row 1.
ui_patterns.why_not_flat: A card grid forces the eye to read every box to find anything. A sorted table imposes a 1-dimensional ranking: the thing you care about (busiest / mine / on this port) is deterministically at the top, and columns let the eye scan straight down a single attribute instead of re-parsing each card.

ui_patterns.pattern: Tree / grouped view with collapsible parents (indentation + twisties)
ui_patterns.description: htop's F5 tree view and btop's tree toggle indent child processes under their parent with ASCII branch glyphs (├─ └─) and a [+]/[-] collapse marker. Windows 11 Task Manager does the consumer version: apps are grouped under an expandable parent row (chevron twisty) with a category band - 'Apps', then 'Background processes', then 'Windows processes' - and View > Group by type / Expand all / Collapse all. Collapsing a noisy parent hides a dozen children behind one summary row.
ui_patterns.why_not_flat: Grouping is the single biggest antidote to a 33-item wall. It splits 'signal' (the user's apps) from 'noise' (OS/system entries) into labelled bands, and collapsing lets a whole category shrink to one line - so the list's visual weight scales with attention, not with raw process count.

ui_patterns.pattern: Per-row inline sparkline / mini-bar in the cell
ui_patterns.description: btop can draw a tiny braille CPU graph per process row (Show CPU graph for selected/each process), and its CPU/mem boxes show a small history sparkline. htop and Task Manager render CPU%/MEM as an inline horizontal meter bar inside the cell rather than a bare number. The bar fills left-to-right proportional to load, so magnitude is preconscious - you see the long bars before you read the numbers.
ui_patterns.why_not_flat: A column of identical-looking numbers is still flat; a column of bars/sparklines has visual relief - tall bars pop out of a field of short ones. It encodes a second dimension (magnitude, or recent-activity-over-time) into the same row height without adding a column.

ui_patterns.pattern: Heat-map cell shading (value-driven background tint)
ui_patterns.description: Windows 11 Task Manager shades each resource cell with the accent color - lighter tint = light load, darker/more-saturated = heavy load - so the whole Processes grid reads as a heat map you can squint at. btop applies a gradient to the process list: rows/values gradient-colour from cool (low CPU) through to hot red (high CPU). The colour is computed from the value, not assigned by category.
ui_patterns.why_not_flat: Colour becomes a sortable visual signal even before you sort. In a flat grid every cell is the same colour; heat-shading makes the 2-3 processes that actually matter glow against a calm background, which is exactly the signal-vs-noise problem PortPilot has.

ui_patterns.pattern: Persistent select-row-to-detail (master-detail), not modal
ui_patterns.description: Activity Monitor: double-click (or select + 'i') a process to open an inspector showing full path, parent PID, open files/ports, sampled stack, energy. btop: select a row, press Enter to expand a detail pane with full command line and per-process graph. The list stays visible; detail is a docked side/bottom panel or inline expansion, not a context-switch to another screen.
ui_patterns.why_not_flat: The truncated COMMAND line in PortPilot's cards is the classic 'where do I put the long stuff' problem. Master-detail keeps the dense scannable list intact and parks all the verbose per-item data (full command, cwd, PID tree, uptime) in one reusable panel that updates as you arrow through rows.

ui_patterns.pattern: Always-on filter/search that narrows the same table in place
ui_patterns.description: htop F4 'incremental filter' and btop's '/' filter both narrow the live table as you type, without leaving the view; Task Manager and Activity Monitor have a top search box doing the same. Crucially the filter operates on the already-grouped, already-sorted table - it doesn't open a separate results screen.
ui_patterns.why_not_flat: It lets one dense surface serve both 'show me everything' and 'show me just :3000 / just node' without a second view. PortPilot already has a filter input; the lesson is to keep it inline over a structured table rather than over a card grid.

ui_patterns.pattern: Status conveyed by glyph + colour token, not just presence
ui_patterns.description: Task Manager flags Efficiency-mode processes with a green leaf and suspended UWP apps with a pause icon; htop colours running threads green and high-priority red; btop dims idle and brightens active. Status is a small leading glyph/dot plus a colour, read before the text.
ui_patterns.why_not_flat: PortPilot currently has no status concept - every port looks 'present' and equal. A leading status dot (green=my-app-running, grey=system, amber=conflict/orphan, red=stoppable) instantly stratifies the wall into meaningful states.

ui_patterns.pattern: Summary meter band pinned above the list
ui_patterns.description: Every one of these tools pins an at-a-glance summary above/around the process table - btop's CPU core meters and mem/net boxes, Activity Monitor's bottom CPU/Memory/Energy tabs with a live graph, Task Manager's coloured per-resource columns header totals. The aggregate lives separately from the per-row detail.
ui_patterns.why_not_flat: It gives the surface two altitudes: a fixed overview strip ('X of my apps running, Y total ports, Z conflicts') above the scrollable detail table - so the user gets orientation before diving into rows, instead of inferring totals from a count badge alone.

steal_these.idea: Replace the two-column card grid with a dense, click-to-sort columns table (PORT | STATUS | PROCESS | PID | OWNER/APP | COMMAND), default-sorted with the user's own dev servers pinned to the top.
steal_these.how: Render the 33 ports as table rows, not cards. Columns are sortable on header click (port asc/desc, process name, PID). The :PORT keeps its large blue treatment but as the leftmost cell, not a card title. Truncated COMMAND becomes one ellipsised column that the detail panel expands. This alone kills most of the flatness.

steal_these.idea: Group rows into collapsible bands: 'My Dev Servers' / 'Other User Ports' / 'System & OS (svchost, System PID 4)' with a chevron and a count per band, system band collapsed by default.
steal_these.how: Classify each scanned port: if its PID/command matches a registered MY APPS entry -> 'My Dev Servers' (always expanded, top). Known OS owners (svchost :135, System :139/:445) -> 'System & OS', collapsed to a single 'System & OS (18)' row. Everything else -> middle band. Borrow Task Manager's Group-by-type / Expand-all / Collapse-all menu. Instantly separates signal from noise.

steal_these.idea: Add a leading status dot + heat-shaded CPU/MEM (or last-seen) cell per row so the busy/mine/conflict rows visually pop.
steal_these.how: Status dot: green=registered app currently running on a live port, grey=system, amber=port conflict or orphaned (registered app expected here but a different process holds it), red-on-hover=killable. If process CPU/mem is available from the scan, shade that cell btop/Task-Manager style (cool->hot). Even without CPU, shade by category so the table reads as a quick heat map.

steal_these.idea: Merge MY APPS and ACTIVE PORTS into one reconciled view via the master-detail pattern instead of two disconnected tabs.
steal_these.how: The 'My Dev Servers' band IS the My Apps list, but augmented with live port reality: each registered app row shows its live :PORT and a green running dot when matched to a scan result, or a grey 'stopped' + Start button when not. Selecting a row opens the detail panel with start/stop controls, full command, cwd, and uptime. 'Is my app running and on which port' becomes one glance, one row.

steal_these.idea: Add a docked detail panel (right side on desktop/web, inline expand in the VS Code tree) that updates on row select - full command, cwd, PID, uptime, copy/kill/open actions live here.
steal_these.how: Select any port/app row -> right-hand panel populates (Activity Monitor inspector style). This is where the full untruncated COMMAND, working directory, PID tree, and the copy/kill/open-in-browser buttons live, de-cluttering each row. In the VS Code extension, reuse the native tree's expand-to-reveal + hover inline actions to mirror it.

steal_these.idea: Convert the horizontal top-tabs to a left vertical nav (icon+label rail) and convert Settings' flat box-stack into a two-pane settings layout (sub-nav list + detail).
steal_these.how: Left rail: Ports / Apps / Knowledge / Settings as a vertical icon list (scales past 5, mirrors btop/Task-Manager region paradigm and the VS Code activity bar you already have). Settings becomes left sub-nav (Theme | Preferences | Data) + right detail pane, so Theme swatches, scan-interval, and export/import each get their own focused panel instead of a long scroll of full-width bordered boxes.

steal_these.idea: Pin a compact summary band above the list (counts + a small live meter) as a second altitude.
steal_these.how: Above the table: 'N my-apps running / M total ports / K conflicts' as small stat chips, plus an optional sparkline of scan-over-time activity. Replaces the lone '33 ports' badge with an orientation strip, matching the overview-band-above-detail-table convention every process monitor uses.

status_visualization: Process monitors avoid a binary running/stopped flag and instead layer three independent status channels: (1) a leading glyph/dot for discrete state - Task Manager's green leaf (efficiency), pause icon (suspended), htop's green/red thread colours; (2) value-driven heat shading of resource cells - Task Manager's accent-tint heat map and btop's cool->hot gradient encode magnitude as colour so heavy items glow; (3) sort position itself as status - CPU-descending sort means 'the thing eating your machine' is structurally always row 1. For PortPilot this maps to a 4-state dot (green=my-app-running, grey=system/OS, amber=conflict/orphaned, red=killable-on-hover), optional cool->hot shading on a CPU/last-activity cell, and a default sort that floats the user's own running dev servers above the OS noise - turning 33 identical boxes into a stratified, glanceable list.
density_and_hierarchy: These tools handle hundreds of items where PortPilot has 33, so their density techniques have huge headroom. The core moves, in order of impact for PortPilot: (1) Tables over cards - columns let the eye scan one attribute vertically instead of re-reading every card; row height shrinks so 33 items fit without scrolling. (2) Collapsible category bands (Task Manager Apps/Background/Windows, htop tree collapse) - the dominant fix; the OS-port noise collapses to a single summary row, so visual weight tracks attention not count. (3) Master-detail - verbose per-item data (full command, cwd, PID tree) moves out of the row into a shared panel, keeping rows thin and scannable. (4) Inline sparklines/heat shading add a magnitude dimension inside existing row height (no extra columns). (5) In-place filter narrows the same structured table rather than spawning a second view. btop also shows progressive disclosure - boxes toggle on/off (keys 1-5,d) and any widget expands to fullscreen with 'e' - a pattern PortPilot can borrow as 'expand the ports table to fill the window, collapse the summary band'. Virtualization is not needed at 33 rows but the table structure makes it free if app/port counts grow.
caveats: Do not copy the TUI aesthetic literally - braille/ASCII graphs, gradient ramps over every value, and 6-region keyboard-toggle layouts are dazzling in a terminal but become noisy chartjunk in an Electron/web GUI; use restrained dot+badge+single-bar, not full btop gradients on a desktop app. Do not add real-time CPU/MEM sparklines unless the scan actually samples those metrics cheaply - PortPilot scans ports, it isn't a process profiler, and faking per-process CPU graphs would be misleading and costly; if no live metric exists, shade by category/status instead of inventing load graphs. Don't over-engineer sorting/columns the user will never use (USER, PRIORITY, NICE, threads) - keep to PORT/STATUS/PROCESS/PID/APP/COMMAND. Heat-map shading must respect the chosen theme (6 themes including light ones) - a gradient tuned for Brutalist Dark will be illegible on Solarized/Brutalist Light, so derive shading from theme tokens, not hardcoded reds. Finally, keyboard-centric navigation (s to sort, / to filter, e to expand) is great as an accelerator but must not be the only path in a GUI - back every shortcut with a clickable control.
applicability_reason: Process monitors solve PortPilot's exact stated problem - making a high-density list of start/stop/inspect-able services scannable instead of a flat uniform wall - via directly transplantable patterns (sortable grouped tables, collapsible OS-vs-mine bands, status dots, master-detail, heat shading), and they even share PortPilot's three-surface reality (TUI/desktop/embedded), with the only non-applicable parts being literal terminal aesthetics and live-CPU graphs PortPilot doesn't measure.

tool: Vercel, Railway, and Render web dashboards (deployment/infrastructure PaaS dashboards)
one_liner: Three PaaS dashboards that render "running infrastructure with live state" as status-pilled service rows/cards, a master-detail drill-in, and (Railway) a spatial canvas graph — the reference class for turning a flat list of start/stop/inspect items into a scannable hierarchy.

ui_patterns.pattern: Status pill as the primary visual anchor (color + word + dot)
ui_patterns.description: Vercel renders deployment state as a small rounded pill with a colored dot + label: Ready = green dot/checkmark, Building = animated/pulsing amber/yellow with a spinner, Error = red, Queued = grey, Canceled = grey-strikethrough. The pill sits left of or beside the deployment name so your eye lands on STATE first, name second. Render does the same with 'Live' (green), 'Deploying' (blue/animated), 'Build failed'/'Deploy failed' (red), 'Suspended' (grey). The word and the color are redundant on purpose (colorblind-safe) and the dot animates while transitional.
ui_patterns.why_not_flat: State becomes the loudest pixel on each item, so a list of 30 items reads as 'mostly green, two red, one pulsing' at a glance instead of 30 equal-weight name strings. Color does the triage the eye otherwise can't.

ui_patterns.pattern: Master-detail drill-in (list row -> full service detail page)
ui_patterns.description: Every service in Render/Railway/Vercel is a row/card in a list, but clicking it opens a dedicated detail surface with its own left sub-nav or tab strip: Overview / Deployments / Logs / Metrics / Environment / Settings. The list view is deliberately sparse (name, status, last-deploy, region/branch); all density moves into the detail page. Breadcrumb at top (Project > Service > Tab) lets you climb back.
ui_patterns.why_not_flat: Splits a flat info-dump into two altitudes: a scannable index and a deep single-item workspace. The list stays calm because detail is one click down, not crammed into the row. This is the antidote to PortPilot's 'everything on one card' flatness.

ui_patterns.pattern: Railway's spatial canvas / service graph with dependency edges
ui_patterns.description: Railway's default project view is a zoomable/pannable canvas where each service is a draggable rounded node (custom devicon, name, latest deploy status dot, and a tiny metrics sparkline strip on the card). Nodes are connected by curved edges that represent reference-variable / network relationships (e.g. an app node wired to its Postgres node). You arrange them spatially; position is persisted. Real-time: deploy state and logs update live on the nodes without reload.
ui_patterns.why_not_flat: Topology and relationships are encoded in 2D space and edges, not inferred from a sorted list. 'What talks to what' and 'what's the shape of my stack' become legible. Grouping is spatial rather than a flat alphabetical column.

ui_patterns.pattern: Grouped containers: Project > Environment > Service hierarchy
ui_patterns.description: Render groups services under Projects, and each project holds Environments (Production / Staging) as tabs or columns; services live inside an environment. Railway scopes everything to an Environment selector (a dropdown/pill in the top bar) — switching it re-scopes the whole canvas. Environment Groups (Render) / Shared Variables (Railway) are first-class grouped containers shown as their own panel.
ui_patterns.why_not_flat: Introduces 2-3 levels of nesting so items are never shown as one giant undifferentiated set. A scope switcher at the top means the same surface shows different subsets, replacing 'show everything always.'

ui_patterns.pattern: Environment-variable manager: table + per-row reveal + Raw Editor toggle
ui_patterns.description: Railway/Render env UIs are a two-column KEY / VALUE table. Values are masked (••••) with a per-row eye toggle to reveal, a copy icon, and inline edit. A 'Raw Editor' toggle flips the whole table into a .env textarea for bulk paste/edit, then parses back to rows on save. Railway adds reference chips: typing ${{ triggers an autocomplete of other services' vars, and a referenced value renders as a colored chip linking to its source service. 'Sealed' vars show a lock icon and are permanently un-revealable.
ui_patterns.why_not_flat: Two modes (structured rows vs raw text) serve scanning AND bulk editing without compromise. Masking + reveal-on-demand keeps secrets quiet by default. Reference chips turn opaque strings into navigable links between items.

ui_patterns.pattern: Metadata strip + last-event line under each item name
ui_patterns.description: Each Vercel deployment row carries a secondary line: commit message, branch (git icon), author avatar, and a relative timestamp ('Updated 3m ago'). Render shows 'Deployed <commit> · <time>' and the region/instance type as muted sub-text. Typography is tiered: name in medium weight near-white, metadata in smaller muted grey.
ui_patterns.why_not_flat: Two-tier typography per item creates a primary/secondary read inside a single row — you scan names, then drop to metadata only on the one you care about. Eliminates the 'every word same size/weight' flatness PortPilot has with its PROCESS/PID/COMMAND lines.

ui_patterns.pattern: Inline row actions revealed on hover + overflow (...) menu
ui_patterns.description: List rows are clean by default; hovering reveals action icons (open ↗, redeploy ↻, logs, stop), and a trailing kebab/overflow menu holds the rest (rollback, delete, settings). Destructive actions (delete/suspend) live in the overflow and often require a typed-confirm modal, never a bare always-visible button.
ui_patterns.why_not_flat: Keeps the resting state uncluttered so status/name dominate, and demotes the dangerous 'kill' action out of the always-visible layer. PortPilot currently shows a bare red X on every one of 33 cards — including OS ports you must not kill.

ui_patterns.pattern: Live metrics sparklines embedded on the card/node
ui_patterns.description: Railway nodes and Render service cards show a tiny inline CPU/memory/network sparkline or a small ring, updating in near-real-time. The detail view expands these into full time-series graphs with a range picker. The card-level spark is glanceable health, not precise readout.
ui_patterns.why_not_flat: Adds a quantitative dimension (is this thing busy/healthy?) to each item without adding a row, so the list carries more signal per pixel while still scanning cleanly.

ui_patterns.pattern: Empty/transitional states with skeletons and progress affordance
ui_patterns.description: While building, Vercel/Render show an animated progress state on the item (spinner, 'Building…' with a live-updating elapsed timer, streaming log preview). Empty projects show a centered illustration + primary CTA ('Create your first service') rather than a blank grid.
ui_patterns.why_not_flat: Time-based states get their own visual treatment so a transitioning item is unmistakably different from a steady one — motion signals 'this is changing right now.'

steal_these.idea: Add a status concept to ports and render it as a colored pill+dot, then sort/group by it
steal_these.how: PortPilot currently has NO status concept — every port is visually equal. Derive a status per port: 'My dev server' (green, matches a MY APPS entry or known dev runtime like node/vite/next), 'Running-unmanaged' (blue, a dev-ish process not registered), 'System/OS' (grey, svchost/System/PID 4). Render each as a Vercel-style pill on the left edge of the card. Then group the wall of 33 into sections: 'Your apps' (top, green) / 'Other dev ports' (blue) / 'System ports' (collapsed grey accordion). Color does the signal-vs-noise triage the user explicitly asked for.

steal_these.idea: Merge Active Ports + My Apps into one master list keyed on the app, with live-port binding
steal_these.how: The user's pain is that 'is my registered app running, and on which port' is split across two tabs. Follow Render's model where a service row shows both its definition AND its live state. Make MY APPS the master list; each app row shows a Live/Stopped pill and, when live, the actual bound port (':3000') pulled from the active-ports scan. Unregistered active ports appear in a second 'Unmanaged ports' group below. One surface answers definition + runtime together.

steal_these.idea: Master-detail drill-in for a port/app instead of cramming everything on the card
steal_these.how: PortPilot has no detail view — PROCESS/PID/COMMAND are all jammed onto the flat card. Adopt the Render pattern: card shows only port, status pill, process name, and a one-line truncated command. Clicking opens a detail panel (right-side drawer fits Electron better than a full route) with tabs: Overview (full command, cwd, uptime, PID tree), Logs (if it's a managed app), Actions (stop/kill/open-in-browser/copy). Density moves down a level; the list stays calm.

steal_these.idea: Replace horizontal top-tabs with a left icon-rail + collapsible grouped sidebar
steal_these.how: The current horizontal tabs (ACTIVE PORTS | MY APPS | KNOWLEDGE | SETTINGS) eat vertical space and won't scale past ~5. Copy Render/Railway's left vertical nav: a slim icon rail (ports, apps, knowledge, settings) that frees vertical space for the dense list, and lets you nest (e.g. Settings expands into Theme/Preferences/Data sub-items inline) without a second tab row. Mirrors the VS Code extension's activity-bar+sidebar shape, unifying the two surfaces' mental models.

steal_these.idea: Status-grouped header counts + a real status summary in the bar
steal_these.how: Replace the bare '33 ports' badge with a segmented count like Vercel/Render summaries: '3 your apps · 5 dev · 25 system'. Color each segment. This becomes the at-a-glance health line and maps directly to the VS Code 'PP: N running' status-bar counter — make both report the same managed-running number so the three surfaces agree.

steal_these.idea: Settings as a two-pane sub-nav (left section list, right panel), not a flat vertical stack
steal_these.how: Render/Railway settings are a left list (General, Environment, Variables, Danger) + right detail pane. PortPilot's Settings is a flat stack of full-width boxes. Split it: left rail items Theme / Preferences / Data (and future: Scan rules, Knowledge); right pane shows the selected section. Theme swatches become a proper preview grid (each swatch shows a mini-UI preview like Railway's icon picker), not 6 bare buttons.

steal_these.idea: Demote the destructive 'kill' action into hover/overflow with a confirm, especially for system ports
steal_these.how: Every PortPilot card has an always-visible red X — dangerous next to OS ports (:135, :445, PID 4) where killing can destabilize Windows. Follow the hover-reveal + overflow pattern: hide kill behind hover; for system-classified ports, gate it behind a typed/confirm modal and a warning ('This is a Windows system process'). Copy stays one-click; kill earns friction proportional to risk.

steal_these.idea: Reference-chip + masked-reveal treatment for any future env/config surface
steal_these.how: If PortPilot ever surfaces per-app env vars or start-command secrets, adopt Railway's masked value with eye-toggle + copy + a Raw Editor toggle for bulk paste. Even now, the single shared JSON config could get an 'Edit raw' toggle in the Data section (structured form vs raw JSON textarea), giving power users bulk edit while keeping the form for everyone else.

status_visualization: The defining move across all three is the colored status pill: a small rounded chip with a leading dot + word, where color is redundant with the label (colorblind-safe) and the dot animates while transitional. Vercel: Ready=green, Building=pulsing amber+spinner, Error=red, Queued/Canceled=grey. Render: Live=green, Deploying=blue animated, Build/Deploy failed=red, Suspended=grey. Railway pushes status onto canvas nodes as a dot + live sparkline, updating in real time without reload. Three reusable principles for PortPilot: (1) state is the loudest pixel, placed first in reading order; (2) motion encodes transitional states (building/starting) so 'changing right now' is unmistakable; (3) word+color+dot triple-encode so the list triages at a glance — 'mostly green, two red, one pulsing.' PortPilot has zero status today; even a 3-state pill (your-app green / dev blue / system grey) would transform the flat wall.
density_and_hierarchy: These dashboards beat flatness with four stacked techniques. (1) Nesting containers: Project > Environment > Service, so items are never one giant set — there's always a parent scope. (2) A scope switcher (Railway's environment pill, Render's project/env tabs) re-scopes the whole surface, replacing 'show everything always' with 'show the relevant subset.' (3) Master-detail: the list view is deliberately sparse (name, status pill, one metadata line) and ALL density moves into a per-item detail page with its own tab strip — two altitudes instead of one crammed card. (4) Tiered typography per row: name in medium near-white, metadata (commit/branch/time/region) in smaller muted grey, so each row has a primary and secondary read. Railway additionally offers spatial grouping via the canvas (drag-arrange, persisted position) as an alternative to linear lists entirely. For PortPilot's ~33 ports the highest-leverage borrow is status-grouping into collapsible sections (Your apps / Dev / System-collapsed) plus the sparse-row + drill-in detail drawer — that alone converts the uniform grid into a scannable, signal-first hierarchy.
caveats: Do NOT copy the full PaaS heaviness. (1) Railway's canvas/graph is seductive but overkill for localhost ports — dev servers rarely have meaningful inter-port edges, and a draggable spatial canvas is a lot of engineering for a vanilla-JS renderer; treat it as inspiration for grouping/node-cards, not a literal feature to build. Reserve any graph idea for showing app->declared-dependency relationships only if that data exists. (2) Environments (Production/Staging) don't map to a single-machine localhost manager — don't invent an environment switcher with no underlying concept; the analogous axis is status-group, not environment. (3) Deployment-centric chrome (build logs, regions, redeploy, rollback, health checks) is irrelevant — a port either exists or doesn't; don't bolt on a fake build pipeline. (4) Sealed/reference variables and the full env-table are over-engineering unless PortPilot genuinely gains per-app secrets; the masked-reveal + Raw Editor toggle is the only piece worth keeping, applied to the existing JSON config. (5) Live metrics sparklines require sampling per-PID CPU/mem on Windows every interval — nice-to-have, real cost, and risky on a no-framework renderer; defer. (6) These are dark, brand-heavy SaaS UIs — PortPilot already has a 6-theme system (TokyoNight/Nord/Dracula etc.), so steal the structure/hierarchy patterns, not the specific Vercel-black/Railway-purple palette.
applicability_reason: PortPilot's exact stated pain (a flat wall of equal items, no status, no grouping, definition split from runtime) is the precise problem these PaaS dashboards solved with status pills, grouped containers, and master-detail — a near-perfect shape match — minus deployment-specific machinery that doesn't apply to localhost.

tool: Git GUI clients: Fork, Tower, GitHub Desktop (three-pane master-detail shell)
one_liner: Desktop Git clients that turn a huge, messy pile of refs/commits/changes into a calm three-pane shell: a grouped collapsible sidebar (the navigator), a scannable middle list (the items), and a rich detail pane (the inspector) — exactly the hierarchy PortPilot's flat grid lacks.

ui_patterns.pattern: Three-pane master-detail shell (navigator | list | inspector)
ui_patterns.description: Fork and Tower both run a fixed three-column layout: a narrow left sidebar of refs (Local/Remotes/Tags/Stashes), a center commit-history list (the master), and a right/bottom detail pane showing the selected commit's metadata + file list + diff (the inspector). Selecting in the sidebar reframes the list; selecting in the list populates the inspector. GitHub Desktop is the simplified two-pane variant: a left rail with a History/Changes toggle + commit list, and a large right diff pane. The panes are resizable with draggable splitters and remember their widths.
ui_patterns.why_not_flat: Instead of one giant uniform surface, information is split by ROLE across three zones with a clear left-to-right drill path (pick a scope, pick an item, inspect it). Depth comes from the selection cascade: the same screen shows context, list, and detail simultaneously without modal hops.

ui_patterns.pattern: Grouped, collapsible sidebar with type headers and live counts
ui_patterns.description: Fork's left sidebar is divided into labelled, collapsible groups: LOCAL, REMOTES (each remote nests its own branches in a tree), TAGS, STASHES. Each group header is uppercase/muted, has a disclosure triangle, and can show a count or collapse to a single line. Tower does the same with Branches/Tags/Submodules/Stashes/Remotes. The current branch is bold with a checkmark/HEAD marker; branches with unpushed/unpulled work show small ahead/behind arrow counts (↑2 ↓1) inline on the right edge of the row.
ui_patterns.why_not_flat: This is the single most direct fix for PortPilot's wall: items are partitioned into named TYPE buckets the user can collapse to hide noise. Counts on headers let you assess a whole group at a glance without expanding it, and the ahead/behind badges put per-row status inline rather than in a separate view.

ui_patterns.pattern: Branch-name folder nesting from slashes
ui_patterns.description: Fork and Tower parse '/' in branch names (feature/login, release/2.0) into an actual collapsible folder tree inside the LOCAL group, so feature/login and feature/signup sit under a 'feature' folder you can fold away.
ui_patterns.why_not_flat: Turns a long flat alphabetical list into a shallow hierarchy that mirrors how the user mentally groups work — auto-derived from existing naming, zero manual setup.

ui_patterns.pattern: Pinned/favorited items float above the rest
ui_patterns.description: Tower lets you mark favorite branches/repos that pin to the top of the sidebar; Fork keeps the current HEAD branch visually distinguished. Frequently-touched refs get a star and a reserved top slot, separated from the long tail by a subtle divider.
ui_patterns.why_not_flat: Creates a two-tier importance hierarchy in the same list — 'mine/active' on top, 'everything else' below — instead of treating every row as equal.

ui_patterns.pattern: Toolbar with semantically grouped, icon+label action clusters
ui_patterns.description: All three put a top toolbar with actions grouped by function and separated by thin vertical dividers: a sync cluster (Pull, Push, Fetch — each an icon+text button, Push showing a count badge of unpushed commits), a branch cluster (Branch, Merge, Rebase, Stash), and a right-aligned search/filter. GitHub Desktop compresses this to three big split-buttons (Current Repository ▾, Current Branch ▾, Fetch/Pull/Push contextual button) whose label text changes to the next sensible action and whose subtitle shows counts ('Push 3 commits to origin').
ui_patterns.why_not_flat: Actions are chunked into meaningful clusters rather than a flat row of equal buttons, and the primary button is context-aware (it tells you both what it'll do and the magnitude), so the toolbar communicates state, not just affordances.

ui_patterns.pattern: Selection-driven detail/inspector pane with tabbed sub-views
ui_patterns.description: Clicking a commit fills the inspector: header block (author avatar, full message, SHA, date, parent), then a file-change list (each file with A/M/D status glyph + green/red +/- line counts), then the diff itself. Tower offers History vs Working-Copy modes and tabs the detail between changed-files and diff; the inspector is empty-state-aware ('Select a commit') when nothing is chosen.
ui_patterns.why_not_flat: Per-item depth lives in a dedicated pane that only renders for the selected row, so the list stays scannable and dense while full detail is one click away — progressive disclosure instead of cramming everything into each card.

ui_patterns.pattern: Status conveyed by glyph + color + count, never by row presence alone
ui_patterns.description: Throughout: file status uses colored letter glyphs (green A added, orange M modified, red D deleted, purple R renamed); branch rows show ↑/↓ ahead-behind pills; the commit graph draws colored lane lines connecting commits to show branch topology; conflict/dirty states get a distinct warning color. GitHub Desktop's changes list uses checkboxes + the same A/M/D coloring.
ui_patterns.why_not_flat: Status is a first-class visual layer (color + icon + number) layered onto otherwise-uniform rows, so the eye sorts signal from noise pre-attentively rather than reading every label.

ui_patterns.pattern: Repository switcher as a top-left dropdown header, not a tab
ui_patterns.description: GitHub Desktop's top-left 'Current Repository' dropdown opens a searchable list of repos grouped by type; Fork uses window tabs per repo. The active context is a persistent labelled control, not one of N horizontal tabs competing for space.
ui_patterns.why_not_flat: Replaces horizontal top-tabs (which don't scale past ~5) with a single dropdown control whose label shows the current context — scales to dozens of items and frees the top bar.

ui_patterns.pattern: Filter/quick-search scoped to the active pane
ui_patterns.description: Fork and Tower have a sidebar filter that instantly narrows the ref tree as you type, plus a separate history search that filters the commit list by message/author/SHA/file. Each search affects only its own pane.
ui_patterns.why_not_flat: Filtering is contextual to the zone you're in, so a search narrows the relevant list rather than one global box trying to filter an undifferentiated wall.

steal_these.idea: Adopt the three-pane shell as PortPilot's primary layout: left grouped sidebar (scopes) | middle list (ports/apps) | right inspector (selected item detail).
steal_these.how: Replace the horizontal ACTIVE PORTS|MY APPS|KNOWLEDGE|SETTINGS top-tabs with a left sidebar navigator. The sidebar holds collapsible groups; the middle column is the current list; a right inspector pane shows the selected port/app's full detail. This kills the tab-scaling problem and the flat grid in one move.

steal_these.idea: Group the Active Ports list into collapsible, counted TYPE sections instead of one uniform grid.
steal_these.how: Partition the ~33 ports into headers like MY DEV SERVERS (3), OTHER USER PROCESSES (n), SYSTEM / OS PORTS (n) — derive 'system' from well-known low ports + process names (svchost, System, PID 4). Each header is uppercase/muted with a disclosure triangle and a live count badge; collapse SYSTEM by default so the noise folds to a single line, exactly like Fork's Stashes/Remotes groups. This is the headline fix for 'a wall of 33 equal boxes'.

steal_these.idea: Merge My Apps and Active Ports into one reconciled view using the sidebar-scope pattern.
steal_these.how: Make the sidebar groups be MY APPS (registered projects), RUNNING (live ports matched to apps), and UNMANAGED PORTS. A registered app row shows its live port + ahead/behind-style status inline (running on :3000 green dot vs stopped grey dot) by matching config to scanned ports — so 'is my app running and where' is answered in ONE view, mirroring how Tower shows branch + its ahead/behind in the same row.

steal_these.idea: Put per-row status as glyph+color+count, and float the user's real dev servers to the top.
steal_these.how: Give each port/app row a left status dot (green running / grey stopped / red conflict) plus inline metadata pills (PID, framework, uptime). Pin favorited/registered apps to the top above a divider, push OS ports to a collapsed group at the bottom — recreating Fork's HEAD-branch-distinguished + favorites-on-top two-tier hierarchy so signal sits above noise.

steal_these.idea: Build a real inspector pane for the selected port/app instead of cramming everything onto each card.
steal_these.how: Clicking a row opens a right inspector: big :PORT header, process tree, full (untruncated) command, working dir, framework guess, log tail, and the copy/kill/open actions as a grouped action bar. The middle list rows then get DENSER (one line each: dot, :port, process, tiny command) because depth moved to the inspector — progressive disclosure like the commit-detail pane.

steal_these.idea: Convert Settings from a flat stack of full-width boxes into a sidebar-nav settings surface with grouped sections.
steal_these.how: When SETTINGS is the active sidebar scope, the middle column becomes a sub-nav (Appearance / Scanning / Data) and the right pane shows that section's controls. Theme swatches become a labelled Appearance group; Auto-scan + interval a Scanning group; Export/Import a Data group — a two-level hierarchy instead of one vertical pile.

steal_these.idea: Replace the SCAN PORTS / ADD APP top buttons with a context-aware grouped toolbar.
steal_these.how: Group toolbar actions like the Git clients: a scan cluster (Scan, with a 'last scanned 12s ago' subtitle + count badge of new ports found), an add cluster (Add App), and a right-aligned pane-scoped filter. Make the primary button report magnitude (GitHub Desktop's 'Push 3 commits' → PortPilot's 'Scan — 2 new ports') so the toolbar shows state, not just affordances.

status_visualization: Git clients almost never rely on a separate 'status screen'; status is layered onto the rows themselves. Three layers worth copying: (1) COLOR+GLYPH per item — file status as colored A/M/D letters, branch state as a checkmark/HEAD marker; PortPilot maps this to a left status dot (green running, grey stopped, red conflict/port-collision) plus a type glyph distinguishing dev-server vs OS process. (2) INLINE COUNT BADGES — Fork/Tower's ↑2 ↓1 ahead/behind pills and Push's unpushed-commit badge; PortPilot maps this to a header count per group ('SYSTEM (24)') and per-row metadata pills (PID, uptime, framework). (3) AGGREGATE in the chrome — GitHub Desktop's Push button subtitle and PortPilot's existing 'PP: N running' status-bar counter and VS Code 'N running' badge are the same idea; keep and extend it so the window-level chrome always shows running-count and conflict-count. The key principle: a flat wall has no status because every row looks identical; these tools make status a pre-attentive color/icon/number layer so you scan groups and dots, not labels.
density_and_hierarchy: Git clients routinely hold thousands of commits, dozens of branches, and hundreds of changed files without going flat, via five mechanisms PortPilot can lift directly. (1) TYPE GROUPING with collapsible headers folds whole categories (Remotes, Tags, Stashes) to one line — PortPilot folds SYSTEM/OS ports the same way so 24 noise rows become one collapsed header. (2) MASTER-DETAIL means the dense list rows stay one-line-thin (depth lives in the inspector), so you can show many more items per screen than PortPilot's two-column card grid — cards waste vertical space, single-line rows don't. (3) SLASH-NESTING and folders add a shallow tree so a long list reads as a few groups of a few items. (4) PINNING/FAVORITES create a two-tier 'mine vs everything' split. (5) PROGRESSIVE DISCLOSURE: collapsed-by-default noise, expand-on-demand detail, lazy-rendered diffs. Net: PortPilot's 33-card wall becomes ~3 dev-server rows on top + a couple of collapsible noise groups below, with full per-port detail one click away in the inspector — high density AND clear hierarchy. Watch virtualization: 33 ports needs none, but the same row-list pattern scales if a machine has hundreds of listeners.
caveats: Don't over-copy the heaviness. (1) The commit-GRAPH (colored topology lanes) is Git-specific and has no PortPilot analog — skip it; ports have no parent/child lineage. (2) Full three-pane (sidebar + list + inspector) can feel cramped in PortPilot's smaller Electron window and especially in the VS Code sidebar surface, which is narrow and vertical — there, collapse to the GitHub Desktop two-pane (or keep the existing two tree-views) rather than forcing three columns. (3) Don't replicate Git's modal-heavy action dialogs (rebase/merge wizards); PortPilot actions (start/stop/kill) are one-shot and should stay inline hover buttons, not multi-step flows. (4) Tower/Fork assume a always-present detail pane; for a glanceable port manager, make the inspector collapsible so power users can run list-only. (5) Resist importing Git terminology or the dense pro-tool chrome wholesale — PortPilot's audience wants 'which of my servers is up', not a 14-button toolbar; group actions but keep the count small. (6) The system-vs-dev port classification is heuristic (process name + port range); show it as a sensible default grouping the user can override, not as ground truth — mislabeling a user's server as 'system' would hide it, which is worse than the current flat wall.
applicability_reason: PortPilot's exact problems — a flat undifferentiated list of start/stop/inspect items, navigation that won't scale past a few tabs, no grouping of signal vs noise, and app-vs-port state split across views — are precisely the problems the Git-client three-pane shell (grouped collapsible sidebar + dense list + selection inspector) was built to solve, and almost every pattern maps onto a concrete PortPilot surface.

tool: Cross-tool STATE-VISUALIZATION study: Docker Desktop, OrbStack, Vercel, GitHub Actions, Railway, Fly.io, k9s/lazydocker, macOS Activity Monitor, VS Code, Tailscale, Linear, Postman
one_liner: How the best dev/infra tools encode service state (running/stopped/starting/error/conflict) using a small, redundant vocabulary of dots, pills, glyphs, motion and counts - and the coherent status model PortPilot should adopt, since it currently has none (a port is just "in use").

ui_patterns.pattern: Leading status dot as the row's first glyph (Docker Desktop / OrbStack / Tailscale)
ui_patterns.description: Every list row begins with a small filled circle (8-10px) in a fixed left gutter column BEFORE the name: solid green = running, hollow/grey = stopped/exited, amber = starting/unhealthy, red = error. Because the dot sits in its own aligned column, the eye scans a single vertical strip of colour down the left edge and reads 'how many green' in one saccade without parsing any text. OrbStack keeps the dot tiny and native; Docker Desktop uses the same idea but (per its own GitHub issues) the green/grey contrast is too weak - the lesson is to make the OFF state visually distinct by SHAPE (hollow ring) not just a darker green.
ui_patterns.why_not_flat: A flat grid gives every item equal visual weight. A fixed-position colour gutter turns 33 equal boxes into a scannable spectrum: your 2 green dev servers pop out of 31 grey OS dots instantly. Hierarchy comes from colour saturation (saturated = live/important, desaturated = dormant/noise) without any reordering.

ui_patterns.pattern: Status PILL with icon + word, not bare colour (Vercel / GitHub Actions / Railway)
ui_patterns.description: Vercel renders deployment state as a rounded pill containing a coloured glyph AND a word: a filled green dot + 'Ready', a spinning/pulsing amber ring + 'Building', a red filled circle-with-x + 'Error', a hollow grey clock + 'Queued', a grey slash-circle + 'Canceled'. GitHub Actions does the same with shape-coded glyphs: green check (success), red x (failed), amber spinning dot (in progress), grey dot (skipped/neutral). The glyph SHAPE carries the meaning even in greyscale; the word removes all ambiguity; the colour is the fast-path. Three redundant channels (colour, shape, text) = colour-blind safe by construction.
ui_patterns.why_not_flat: PortPilot today shows ':3000' identically whether the port is a healthy dev server or a zombie. A pill ('● Running 3000', '◌ Stopped', '▲ Conflict') adds a second semantic axis the flat card lacks, so two ports on the same number read as completely different states at a glance.

ui_patterns.pattern: Collapsible grouped sections with a count + roll-up status badge on the header (k9s namespaces / Docker Compose stacks / OrbStack groups / Linear)
ui_patterns.description: Items are bucketed under bold section headers - Docker groups containers by Compose 'stack', OrbStack groups by project, Linear groups issues by status. Each header is a sticky bar showing: disclosure triangle, group name, a count chip ('5'), and a roll-up health glyph that summarises the children (all green = green header dot; any child erroring = red dot on the header even when collapsed). Click to collapse; collapsed groups still show their count + worst-child status. k9s/lazydocker do the TUI version: namespaces as headers, a green/red column per pod.
ui_patterns.why_not_flat: This is the single biggest fix for the 'wall of 33'. Grouping ('My Dev Servers' / 'Docker' / 'System & OS' / 'Other') replaces one undifferentiated grid with 3-4 named buckets, and the count+rollup badge lets you collapse 'System & OS (28)' down to one line so the noise literally disappears while still being one click away. Hierarchy is now structural, not just visual.

ui_patterns.pattern: Animated/pulsing indicator reserved ONLY for transient states (Vercel 'Building', GitHub Actions in-progress, Railway deploying)
ui_patterns.description: Motion is rationed: a steady green dot for 'running' does NOT animate (a screen full of pulsing dots is noise), but a TRANSITIONAL state - starting, stopping, deploying, scanning - gets a slow pulse, a rotating ring, or a barber-pole/indeterminate progress bar. Vercel's 'Building' pill has a subtle rotating arc; GitHub's in-progress is a pulsing amber dot. The motion says 'wait, this will change on its own' and stops the instant the state settles.
ui_patterns.why_not_flat: Flat lists have no time dimension - you can't tell a server that's up from one mid-start. A pulse on 'starting' and a barber-pole on the global 'Scanning ports...' gives temporal hierarchy: things that are settling draw the eye, things that are stable recede.

ui_patterns.pattern: Master-detail drawer / expandable row instead of uniform cards (OrbStack 4-tab detail, Docker container Inspect, macOS Activity Monitor double-click)
ui_patterns.description: The list row stays compact (dot, name, port, status, quick actions) and the DETAIL lives in a side drawer or inline expansion: OrbStack's container page has Info / Logs / Terminal / Files tabs; Activity Monitor pops a per-process inspector with CPU/memory/open-files/ports; Docker Desktop slides in logs + stats + the long command. The truncated COMMAND line that bloats every PortPilot card moves into the drawer, where you also surface PID, full path, uptime, parent process, and a 'kill' confirm.
ui_patterns.why_not_flat: PortPilot currently dumps the full truncated command onto every card, making all cards tall and equally heavy. Master-detail makes the row LIGHT (scannable) and the depth ON-DEMAND. One source of truth (a row) expands to richness instead of 33 cards each competing to show everything.

ui_patterns.pattern: Count badges on tabs / nav showing live totals (VS Code activity bar, GitHub PR counts, Docker tray, PortPilot's own 'PP: N running')
ui_patterns.description: Navigation items carry a small superscript/inline count that reflects live state: VS Code's Source Control gauge shows a change count, the activity bar shows error/warning counts, the Docker tray shows running-container count. The number is the at-a-glance KPI so you don't have to open the tab. Critically, the count can be TYPED by colour - a red '2' for conflicts vs a neutral grey total.
ui_patterns.why_not_flat: PortPilot's horizontal tabs are inert labels. Adding live counts ('Active Ports 33', 'My Apps 5 ● 2 running') turns navigation into a dashboard - hierarchy of attention is encoded in the nav itself, and you learn the state before clicking.

ui_patterns.pattern: Sparkline / micro-metric inline in the row (macOS Activity Monitor, Docker Desktop CPU column, Railway/Fly metrics strip)
ui_patterns.description: A tiny 40-60px sparkline or a single live number (CPU %, mem MB) sits in a right-aligned column. Activity Monitor shows per-process CPU as a number that you can sort by; Docker Desktop shows a mini CPU/mem bar per container; Fly/Railway show a sparkline of recent request volume. It's a third data channel that costs almost no width but adds 'is this thing actually doing work or idle'.
ui_patterns.why_not_flat: Not every PortPilot port needs this, but for 'My Apps' that are running, a tiny uptime ('up 2h') or a request-activity sparkline distinguishes a hot dev server from one that started and hung. Adds depth to the running state - 'running' is no longer binary.

ui_patterns.pattern: Settings as left-rail sub-navigation, not a flat scroll of boxes (VS Code Settings, Linear settings, Postman settings, macOS System Settings)
ui_patterns.description: Modern settings use a two-pane layout: a narrow left list of CATEGORIES (Theme, Scanning, Data, Advanced) and a right detail pane that swaps content per category. VS Code adds a search box that filters across all settings and a breadcrumbed table of contents. Linear/Postman group settings under headers with a sticky mini-TOC. Each setting row is label + control + one line of helper text, in a tidy form grid - not a full-width bordered card.
ui_patterns.why_not_flat: PortPilot's Settings is a vertical stack of full-width bordered boxes (Theme, Preferences, Data) - the definition of flat. A left-rail with 4 categories + a search field scales past 3 sections, gives spatial memory ('Theme is top-left'), and lets the theme swatches breathe in a proper grid instead of a cramped box.

steal_these.idea: Adopt an explicit 5-state status model: RUNNING (solid green ●), STOPPED (hollow grey ◌), STARTING/STOPPING (amber pulse ◐), ERROR (red ✕ in circle), CONFLICT/PORT-CLASH (amber triangle ▲). Every port and every app maps to exactly one. This is the foundational missing primitive - PortPilot has no status concept today.
steal_these.how: Define a single statusOf(item) function in renderer.js returning {state, color, glyph, label}. The desktop card, the VS Code tree item (use ThemeIcon with color), and the web portal all read from it so all three surfaces stay identical. Map: a scanned port owned by a known dev process => RUNNING; a registered app with no live port => STOPPED; a registered app whose declared port is taken by a DIFFERENT process => CONFLICT.

steal_these.idea: Put a fixed-position leading status dot in a left gutter on every Active Ports row, and make OFF states differ by SHAPE (hollow ring) not just dimmer colour - the exact accessibility mistake Docker Desktop is criticised for.
steal_these.how: Reserve a 16px left column. Solid filled disc for live dev servers, hollow 1.5px ring for OS/idle ports, so the user's 2 real servers form a bright column against 31 hollow rings. Greyscale-test it: the running vs stopped distinction must survive a desaturate filter because shape differs, not only hue.

steal_these.idea: Group Active Ports into named, collapsible sections with count + roll-up badges instead of one 33-cell grid: 'My Dev Servers', 'Docker', 'System & OS', 'Other'. Default-collapse 'System & OS'.
steal_these.how: Classify by process name/path: node/vite/next/python/etc => Dev; com.docker/dockerd => Docker; svchost/System/PID 4/known OS ports (135/139/445) => System & OS; everything else => Other. Sticky header per group with a disclosure triangle, a count chip, and a worst-child status dot. Persist collapsed state in the JSON config. This single change kills the 'wall of 33' - System & OS (28) collapses to one line.

steal_these.idea: Merge My Apps and Active Ports into ONE reconciled view (or cross-link them) so 'is my registered app running and on which live port' is answered in one place - mirroring how OrbStack/Docker show declared-vs-actual in a single row.
steal_these.how: In My Apps, each app row shows its status dot + the LIVE port it resolved to (from the scan), not just its configured port. If the configured port is held by a foreign process, show the CONFLICT triangle inline with a 'port 3000 taken by chrome.exe - kill?' affordance. Keep My Apps as the primary surface (intent) and let it absorb live scan data rather than forcing a tab switch.

steal_these.idea: Replace the uniform tall cards with compact rows + a master-detail drawer. Move the truncated COMMAND, PID, full path, uptime, and parent process into the drawer; keep the row to dot + :port + process + status-pill + copy/kill.
steal_these.how: Click a row to slide a right-hand drawer (or expand inline). Drawer tabs/sections: Overview (full command, PID, working dir, uptime, owning app if registered), and a 'kill' button with confirm. This lets rows shrink to ~32px so you fit far more on screen, and the depth is on demand - the OrbStack model.

steal_these.idea: Add live, typed count badges to the top-tab navigation and consider moving nav to a left rail (which scales past 5 tabs, unlike the current horizontal gold-underline tabs).
steal_these.how: Tabs become 'Active Ports · 33', 'My Apps · 2/5 running' with a small red count if any CONFLICT exists. A left vertical rail (icon + label + count) reclaims the vertical space the horizontal tabs eat and leaves room for Knowledge/Settings plus future surfaces. The active item gets the gold accent as a left border instead of an underline.

steal_these.idea: Restructure Settings into a left-rail sub-nav (Theme / Scanning / Data / Advanced) with a search field, instead of a vertical stack of full-width bordered boxes.
steal_these.how: Two-pane: category list left, form right. Theme becomes a proper swatch grid with a live mini-preview of a sample card in each theme; Scanning holds auto-scan + interval with helper text; Data holds Export/Import. Add a settings search that filters rows. Scales cleanly when you add more options later.

steal_these.idea: Ration motion: steady dots for stable states, a slow pulse ONLY for STARTING/STOPPING, and a single global barber-pole for the active 'Scanning ports...' pass.
steal_these.how: CSS: .status--starting { animation: pulse 1.2s ease-in-out infinite }. Never animate a running dot. The Scan Ports button shows an indeterminate progress bar while a scan runs, then settles. This gives the UI a time dimension without becoming a disco of blinking lights.

status_visualization: The field has converged on a small, redundant vocabulary - every serious tool uses 2-3 of these channels at once: (1) COLOUR is the fast-path - green=running, grey=stopped, amber=starting/unhealthy/conflict, red=error - but per WCAG 1.4.1 and Docker Desktop's own contrast complaints, colour is never the sole channel. (2) SHAPE/GLYPH carries the meaning in greyscale: filled disc (running) vs hollow ring (stopped), spinning arc (building), circle-x (error), triangle (warning/conflict), slash-circle (canceled/skipped) - GitHub Actions and Vercel both lean on this so it survives colour-blindness and greyscale. (3) TEXT label in a pill removes all ambiguity ('Ready', 'Building', 'Error', 'Queued'). (4) MOTION is reserved strictly for transient states - a pulse or rotating ring means 'this will change on its own', steady states never animate. (5) POSITION - a fixed left-gutter dot lets you read aggregate health down a column without parsing rows. (6) METRICS - sparklines / CPU% / 'up 2h' uptime add a sub-axis so 'running' isn't binary. Roll-up: a group header shows the WORST child status even when collapsed (any red child => red header). For light vs dark themes, the rule is to hold the SEMANTIC hue constant but adjust lightness/saturation for >=3:1 non-text contrast against each theme's background (Carbon/USWDS guidance), and to lean on the shape channel so the system degrades gracefully when a theme washes out a hue. PortPilot has NONE of this today - a port is binary 'in use', no glyph, no group rollup, no motion, no metric.
