density_and_hierarchy: These tools beat the flat-wall problem with five compounding moves, all directly applicable to PortPilot's 33-port grid. (1) GROUPING into named, collapsible sections with count + roll-up badges (Docker Compose stacks, OrbStack projects, k9s namespaces, Linear status groups) - this alone converts 33 equal boxes into 'Dev (2) / Docker (3) / System & OS (28, collapsed) / Other'. (2) DEFAULT-COLLAPSE the noise so OS/system ports are one summary line, not 28 cards - signal/noise separation is structural, not just visual. (3) COMPACT ROWS + MASTER-DETAIL: the list row is ~32px (dot, port, process, status, actions) and the heavy stuff (full command, PID, path, logs, uptime) lives in an on-demand drawer (OrbStack/Activity Monitor/Docker Inspect) - so density goes UP while per-item weight goes DOWN. (4) FIXED-COLUMN ALIGNMENT (status gutter | port | process | metric | actions) so the eye scans vertical strips, not a ragged grid; k9s and Activity Monitor are pure tables for exactly this reason. (5) SORT + SECONDARY GROUPING by importance (favourites/registered apps pinned top, OS ports sunk to a collapsed bottom group) so signal is spatially privileged. PortPilot should NOT virtualize yet - 33 rows is tiny - but the grouped-collapsible-table pattern is what makes a future 100-port machine still legible. The progressive-disclosure ladder is: collapsed group summary -> compact row -> expanded detail drawer, three altitudes instead of one flat plane.
caveats: Do NOT copy these wholesale. (1) Avoid Docker Desktop's actual mistake: its running-green vs stopped-grey dots are too low-contrast and rely on hue alone - if you only dim the colour for 'stopped' you ship the same accessibility bug. Differentiate by shape (filled vs hollow). (2) Don't over-animate: Railway/Vercel pulse only transient states; a PortPilot screen of 33 pulsing dots would be worse than the current flat wall. Steady states must be still. (3) Don't import heavyweight infra metrics - per-container CPU graphs, log streaming, resource charts (Docker Desktop, Fly, Railway) are overkill for a localhost port manager; a single 'up 2h' uptime or a conflict flag is the right altitude. PortPilot is a glanceable utility, not an observability dashboard. (4) Don't blindly adopt a 4-tab OrbStack detail (Info/Logs/Terminal/Files) - PortPilot can't reliably attach to arbitrary foreign processes' logs/terminals, so a single Overview drawer is honest; don't promise tabs you can't fill. (5) Master-detail drawers and left-rail nav add real complexity to a vanilla-HTML/CSS/JS renderer with no framework - the grouping + status-dot + count-badge wins are cheap and high-impact; the drawer and settings sub-nav are the bigger lift, sequence them second. (6) Linear-style polish (smooth section animations, command palette) is aspirational, not load-bearing - don't let it balloon scope on a 16KB/33KB/85KB no-framework codebase.
applicability_reason: PortPilot is structurally the exact shape these tools solve - a list of services you start/stop/inspect with a flat 33-item grid, no status model, split apps-vs-ports views, and a flat settings stack - and the grouped-collapsible-list + redundant-status-vocabulary + master-detail patterns map onto its surfaces almost one-to-one, with the only friction being its no-framework renderer raising the cost of the heavier patterns (drawer, left-rail).

tool: Settings/Preferences UIs — cross-tool study: Raycast, Linear, Arc, macOS System Settings (Ventura), VS Code Settings editor, 1Password
one_liner: Six best-in-class settings surfaces showing how to replace a flat stack of boxes with a searchable left-rail nav, described/sectioned panes, and inline controls (toggles, segmented controls, steppers) that read as a hierarchy instead of a wall.

ui_patterns.pattern: Left-rail category nav with icons + grouped headers (Raycast, macOS Ventura, 1Password)
ui_patterns.description: A fixed left sidebar lists top-level settings categories as icon+label rows (Raycast: Account, General, Extensions, AI, Cloud Sync, Organizations, Advanced, About; macOS: profile chip then Wi-Fi/Bluetooth/Network grouped by faint divider rules). Selecting a row swaps the right pane; the selected row gets a tinted/filled pill background. The rail itself is grouped into labelled clusters with thin separators rather than one long undifferentiated list.
ui_patterns.why_not_flat: Turns a long vertical scroll into a two-pane master/detail: the rail is the always-visible index, the pane shows only one category at a time. Depth comes from the persistent 'where am I' index plus icon scannability, versus PortPilot's current single column of equal full-width boxes you must scroll past.

ui_patterns.pattern: Search-in-settings that filters the whole tree and jumps you to the match (VS Code, macOS, Raycast)
ui_patterns.description: A search field pinned at the top of the settings nav. VS Code's filters the flat settings list live and shows a count; typing '@modified' shows only changed settings; a funnel button offers token filters (@modified, @ext:, @tag:). Raycast's sidebar search finds any command/preference across all categories. Type-ahead narrows hundreds of options to the few that match.
ui_patterns.why_not_flat: Gives a non-spatial path to any setting, so the hierarchy can be deep without being slow. The flat stack has no search because it has few items - but the moment PortPilot adds per-app config, search is the escape hatch that keeps a deeper tree usable.

ui_patterns.pattern: Section header + one-line description under it (1Password, Linear, macOS)
ui_patterns.description: Within a pane, settings are chunked into titled groups: a bold section title, a muted one-line description sentence beneath it, then the controls. 1Password's Security pane: 'Auto-lock' header, grey subtitle 'Lock 1Password after a period of inactivity', then the controls. Linear settings pages lead each group with a short explanatory sentence. macOS uses subtitle text under many rows.
ui_patterns.why_not_flat: The description line does the teaching the current bare 'PREFERENCES' box can't, and the title/description/control rhythm creates visual cadence - eye lands on bold title, reads grey context, acts on control. Three type weights per group replace one flat border box.

ui_patterns.pattern: Inline right-aligned controls on a settings row: toggle / segmented control / stepper (macOS, Linear, 1Password)
ui_patterns.description: Each setting is a single row: label (and optional subtitle) left-aligned, the control right-aligned and vertically centered. Booleans use a switch toggle (not a checkbox); a small set of exclusive options uses a segmented control (a pill split into 2-4 labelled cells, the active cell filled); numeric values use a stepper (a value with up/down chevrons or -/+ caps) or a tidy number field with unit suffix. Rows are separated by hairline insets, not full bordered boxes.
ui_patterns.why_not_flat: Replaces PortPilot's full-width bordered checkbox-and-number-box stack with light hairline-separated rows where the control type signals the data type at a glance. A segmented control for scan-interval presets (Off / 5s / 15s / 30s) reads instantly versus a raw number input.

ui_patterns.pattern: Appearance/theme picker as a visual swatch grid with live preview, not a button list (Arc, VS Code, macOS, 1Password)
ui_patterns.description: Theme pickers show each theme as a miniature rendered preview tile (a tiny mock window in that theme's colours) in a wrapping grid; the selected tile gets a coloured ring/checkmark. macOS shows Light/Dark/Auto as three labelled thumbnail images. Arc shows colour 'spaces' as gradient swatches. VS Code's theme quick-pick previews the theme live as you arrow through the list before committing.
ui_patterns.why_not_flat: PortPilot already has 6 themes but as plain text buttons - upgrading them to preview tiles (each tile painted in its own palette: TokyoNight tile is navy, Solarized tile is cream) makes the grid self-demonstrating and gives the Theme section real visual interest instead of six identical bordered buttons.

ui_patterns.pattern: 'Showing X of Y' / disclosure + collapsible groups (VS Code, macOS, Finder-style)
ui_patterns.description: When a filter or search is active, a count line states the reduced set ('12 of 340 settings'). Long lists use collapsible group headers with a disclosure chevron and a per-group count badge; collapsing a group hides its rows but keeps the header as a spine. VS Code's table-of-contents tree on the left mirrors the right pane and lets you collapse whole categories.
ui_patterns.why_not_flat: Counts and collapsible spines let a dense surface admit how much it's hiding and let users fold away noise. Directly transplants to Active Ports: 'System (28)' collapsed by default, 'My dev servers (5)' expanded - the count badge is the hierarchy signal the flat 33-card grid lacks.

ui_patterns.pattern: Sticky pane header with the category title + primary action (Linear, 1Password, Raycast)
ui_patterns.description: The right pane has its own sticky header: the current category name as an H1, sometimes a short description, and the pane-scoped primary action button top-right (Linear: 'New label' lives in the Labels settings pane header). Content scrolls under it.
ui_patterns.why_not_flat: Establishes a clear second level of title hierarchy (app title > category title > section title) and co-locates the relevant action with its context, versus PortPilot's global top-bar buttons that float disconnected from whichever tab you're on.

ui_patterns.pattern: Master/detail split for items: list on the left, full inspector on the right (1Password, Arc, VS Code keybindings)
ui_patterns.description: 1Password's main view is a two-pane split: vault item list (left, dense rows with icon + title + subtitle) and a read/edit detail panel (right) for the selected item, with fields, copy buttons, and a metadata footer. Selecting a row populates the detail; nothing opens a separate screen. The list rows are compact and scannable; the detail is spacious.
ui_patterns.why_not_flat: This is the single biggest structural lift for PortPilot: a port/app list on the left and a detail inspector on the right (full command, PID, working dir, uptime, kill/open/copy) collapses the disconnected Active Ports grid + My Apps tab into one master/detail surface where 'is my app running and on what port' is answered in one view.

steal_these.idea: Replace the SETTINGS flat stack with a left-rail settings nav (Theme / Scanning / Data / About) + a sticky-headed right pane per category
steal_these.how: Reuse the same two-pane shell you build for ports. Rail rows: Appearance, Scanning, Data & Config, About. Each pane: H1 title, then titled sections with a one-line grey description and hairline-separated rows. Kills the stacked-box look immediately and scales when per-app settings arrive.

steal_these.idea: Section-header + description + inline-control row rhythm inside every settings group
steal_these.how: Auto-scan-on-startup becomes a row: bold 'Auto-scan on startup' + grey 'Scan for active ports when PortPilot launches' + a switch toggle right-aligned. Scan-interval becomes a row with a segmented control (Off / 5s / 15s / 30s) instead of a raw number box. Three type weights per group replace one border.

steal_these.idea: Turn the 6 theme buttons into a swatch-preview grid with live ring-selection
steal_these.how: Render each of TokyoNight/Brutalist Dark/Brutalist Light/Nord/Dracula/Solarized as a small tile painted in that theme's own bg/fg/accent (mini mock of the port card). Selected tile gets a 2px gold ring + check. Trivial in CSS-vars since each theme already defines those variables.

steal_these.idea: Collapsible grouped Active Ports with count badges instead of a uniform 33-card grid
steal_these.how: Group ports by class: 'My dev servers' (matched to registered apps), 'Other user ports', 'System / OS' (svchost, System PID 4 - collapsed by default). Each group is a header row with a disclosure chevron + count badge (e.g. 'System (28)'). Sort dev servers to the top. Signal separates from noise without deleting anything.

steal_these.idea: Search/filter field that filters the grouped tree and shows 'X of Y'
steal_these.how: Keep the existing filter input but make it filter across groups and show a live 'showing 5 of 33' count; add quick token filters (a funnel button: Dev only / Hide system / Listening only) modelled on VS Code's @modified filter chips.

steal_these.idea: Merge Active Ports + My Apps into one master/detail surface
steal_these.how: Left = unified list (registered apps with a live status dot + the port they grabbed, then unmatched live ports below). Right = inspector for the selected row: full command, PID, cwd, uptime, and the start/stop/kill/open/copy actions. Answers 'is my app running and where' in one glance; the separate My Apps tab disappears as a top-level destination.

steal_these.idea: Add a status concept: coloured status dot + label per row (running / stopped / conflict / system)
steal_these.how: Each list row leads with a 8px dot: green=running/listening, grey=stopped, amber=port conflict (two things want the same port), blue/neutral=system. The VS Code 'PP: N running' status-bar counter becomes a small summary chip in the desktop top bar (e.g. '5 running - 1 conflict'). Status is the depth cue the current flat grid completely lacks.

steal_these.idea: Sticky pane header carrying the context-relevant primary action
steal_these.how: When the left-rail/section nav replaces top-tabs, give the right pane a sticky header with the section title and its scoped action - 'Add App' lives in the My Apps pane header, 'Scan Ports' in the Active Ports pane header - instead of two global buttons in the top bar that ignore which surface you're on. Also frees the vertical space the 4 top-tabs eat and scales past 5 destinations.

status_visualization: These tools mostly show config state, not runtime state, so the runtime-status lessons come by analogy. The strongest transferable cue is VS Code's modified-setting indicator: a coloured vertical bar in the left gutter of any row whose value differs from default, plus the '@modified' filter token and a count - a cheap, glanceable 'this is not the baseline' marker. 1Password uses small coloured status chips and a Watchtower badge (red/amber counts) to flag items needing attention. macOS uses inline status text right-aligned on a row (e.g. a network's 'Connected' in muted green). The pattern to lift: a small leading coloured dot + short status word per row (running/stopped/conflict/system) and a single summary chip ('5 running - 1 conflict') in the header - giving PortPilot the running/stopped/error/conflict vocabulary its uniform grid currently has none of. Avoid colour-only encoding; pair every dot with a word for accessibility.
density_and_hierarchy: Settings UIs handle volume with the same three levers PortPilot needs. (1) Master/detail split (Raycast, macOS, 1Password, VS Code): a narrow nav/list index on the left, one detailed pane on the right - only one category's worth of controls is ever on screen, so total item count stops mattering. (2) Two-to-three level sectioning: app-level rail category > pane section header (with description) > individual row, giving three type weights and indent levels so the eye parses structure before content. (3) Progressive disclosure: collapsible groups with count badges (collapse 'System (28)' by default), 'showing X of Y' on filtered views, and search/token-filters as the non-spatial fast path. VS Code additionally mirrors the right-pane sections in a collapsible table-of-contents tree on the left - a true two-way index. For PortPilot's ~33 ports the win is grouping + collapse + a status sort, not virtualization; the list is small but currently undifferentiated, so hierarchy (groups, dots, master/detail) buys far more than raw density tricks.
caveats: Do NOT copy macOS Ventura's mistakes, which are well-documented: it hides the hierarchy (only a tiny back button signals you're a level deep), search drops you into a category without telling you which one you're in, and it over-stuffs 'General' so the rail stays short - all of which would re-flatten PortPilot in a new disguise. Keep the selected rail row clearly highlighted and always show breadcrumbs/section context. Don't over-engineer for PortPilot's scale: it has ~6 themes, ~3 preference groups, ~33 ports - so skip VS Code's heavy split JSON/UI dual-editor, skip deep multi-page settings routing, skip virtualization. A two-pane shell with grouped rows and a swatch theme grid is the right altitude; a full Raycast-style extension-preferences engine is too much. Also resist segmented controls for anything with more than ~4 options (use a dropdown there) and resist toggles for non-boolean state. Finally, the desktop is vanilla HTML/CSS/JS - the two-pane + CSS-variable theme tiles are cheap, but anything requiring a framework (live theme-preview virtualization, complex tree state) should be weighed against the no-framework constraint shared across all three surfaces.
applicability_reason: PortPilot's stated core problem is a flat settings stack and a uniform wall of equal items, and these six tools are the canonical reference set for exactly the cure - searchable left-rail nav, described sections, inline typed controls, swatch theme pickers, and master/detail with status - nearly all of which map directly onto its settings, active-ports, my-apps, navigation, status, and detail-view surfaces.

tool: Cross-tool study: Docker Desktop (Containers view), macOS Activity Monitor / Windows Task Manager, TablePlus/DBeaver connection trees, Postman/Insomnia collections sidebar, VS Code Source Control + Linear/Things grouped lists, k9s/lazydocker TUIs
one_liner: How the best process/service managers and item-list power tools beat the "flat wall of identical rows" by grouping with collapsible counted headers, separating signal from noise, defaulting to sortable tables over card grids, and unifying status into the list itself.

ui_patterns.pattern: Collapsible grouped rows with a counted, summarizing group header (Docker Desktop Containers view)
ui_patterns.description: Docker Desktop renders a flat list of containers, but compose projects collapse into a single parent row: a disclosure triangle, the project name, an aggregate status pill (e.g. 'Running (3/3)'), and ONE set of bulk start/stop/delete actions that act on the whole group. Click the triangle to expand and see the individual containers indented beneath. The header row itself is interactive and summarizes its children, so a 40-container machine reads as 6 project rows until you drill in.
ui_patterns.why_not_flat: The group header is a real, denser unit of information (name + n-of-m running + one action set) that replaces n identical rows with one meaningful row. Collapsing turns an O(items) wall into O(groups) scannable sections, and the aggregate status pill answers 'is this stack up?' without reading every child.

ui_patterns.pattern: Built-in signal/noise filter as a first-class view toggle (Activity Monitor 'System Processes' vs 'Windowed Processes'; Task Manager Apps vs Background processes split)
ui_patterns.description: Activity Monitor's View menu has explicit filters: 'All Processes', 'System Processes', 'My Processes', 'Windowed Processes' (essentially 'things that are real apps'). Windows Task Manager visually splits the same list into a top 'Apps' section and a lower 'Background processes' / 'Windows processes' section under bold dividers. The OS-noise is present but quarantined below or behind a toggle, never interleaved with the things you care about.
ui_patterns.why_not_flat: It encodes a taxonomy (user-owned vs system) directly into the list structure instead of treating every row as equal. The default view surfaces signal; noise is one click or one scroll away. This is the exact fix for PortPilot's :135/:139/:445 svchost/System rows sitting next to :3000 node.

ui_patterns.pattern: Sortable, column-based table as the default density mode, not a card grid (Activity Monitor, Task Manager, k9s, TablePlus result grids)
ui_patterns.description: None of the serious process tools use a 2-column card grid. They use a tight data table: one row per item, fixed columns (Name, PID, % CPU, Port, User), click a column header to sort, click again to reverse, drag to reorder/hide columns. Rows are ~22-28px tall, so 33 items fit on one screen with room to spare and the eye scans a single aligned column (e.g. all ports) vertically.
ui_patterns.why_not_flat: A card grid forces every attribute into a repeated mini-layout, so 33 cards = 33 separate reading tasks with no cross-item alignment. A table makes the columns the hierarchy: you scan one dimension at a time, and sort instantly re-ranks by relevance (port, recency, owner). Cards lose the 'compare across items' affordance entirely.

ui_patterns.pattern: Pinned/favourited items floated to a sticky top section (Things 3 'Today', Linear favorites, TablePlus pinned connections, browser pinned tabs)
ui_patterns.description: A thin always-visible top zone holds user-pinned items above a divider, visually distinct (slightly inset, star-filled icon, sometimes a subtle background tint). The rest of the list scrolls beneath. A star/pin affordance appears on row hover; clicking it lifts that item into the pinned zone and it stays there across refreshes.
ui_patterns.why_not_flat: It lets the user manually promote their 3-4 real dev servers above the churn of ephemeral ports, creating a stable 'these are mine' band that survives rescans. Importance becomes spatial (top = mine) rather than something you re-hunt for every time the port list re-renders.

ui_patterns.pattern: Master-detail (list + inspector panel) instead of cramming everything onto each card (TablePlus, Postman/Insomnia, k9s describe, Proxyman)
ui_patterns.description: Left/main pane is the dense list (just enough to identify and rank: name, port, status). Selecting a row opens a right-side detail panel or bottom drawer with the heavy fields: full command line, working directory, PID tree, env, uptime, logs, copy buttons, kill confirmation. The list stays scannable; depth lives in the panel.
ui_patterns.why_not_flat: PortPilot currently jams PROCESS + PID + truncated COMMAND + copy + kill onto every card, which makes each card heavy AND still truncates the one field (command) you actually open a card to read. Master-detail keeps the list light and gives the full command real room on demand, adding a second altitude of information instead of one flat overloaded level.

ui_patterns.pattern: Sticky group headers + section counts that double as scope for bulk actions (Linear status groups, Finder list view by Kind, VS Code Source Control 'Changes (12)')
ui_patterns.description: Each group header shows label + count badge (e.g. 'Dev servers 4', 'System 9', 'Other 20') and stays pinned to the top of the viewport while you scroll its members. Hovering the header reveals group-scoped actions ('stop all', 'collapse', 'kill group'). Counts update live.
ui_patterns.why_not_flat: The count badge gives an at-a-glance census per category without scrolling, and the header converts a region of the list into an addressable object you can act on or fold away. Scrolling never loses you because the current section's header is always visible at the top edge.

ui_patterns.pattern: Status expressed as a leading colored dot + state word, unified across the whole list (Vercel deployments, GitHub Actions, Docker, Linear)
ui_patterns.description: Every row starts with a small filled circle in a consistent semantic palette: green=running, grey=stopped, amber=starting/conflict, red=error/port-clash. The state is reinforced with a short word so it is not colour-only. Because the dot is always column-1, the eye can vertically scan just the dots to find the one red item among 30 greens.
ui_patterns.why_not_flat: It introduces a status concept where PortPilot currently has none (every card looks 'alive'). A single aligned status column turns 'find the problem' from reading 33 cards into scanning one 4px-wide vertical strip of colour.

ui_patterns.pattern: Sort + filter + saved/segmented views as persistent chips, not a lone text box (Postman, Linear views, browser DevTools network filter chips, email folders)
ui_patterns.description: Above the list: a search box PLUS quick-filter chips ('Mine', 'Listening', 'Node', 'System', 'Conflicts') and a sort dropdown ('Port', 'Recently started', 'CPU'). Selected chips highlight; the active filter/sort persists between sessions. Power users can save a filter combo as a named view in a left rail.
ui_patterns.why_not_flat: PortPilot has only a single filter input and a count badge. Chips turn implicit categories into one-tap lenses, and a remembered default view (e.g. 'Mine, sorted by port') means the user lands on signal every launch instead of re-filtering the 33-item wall by hand.

ui_patterns.pattern: Settings as a two-pane category list + detail pane, not a vertical stack of full-width boxes (VS Code Settings, macOS System Settings, Slack preferences)
ui_patterns.description: Left rail lists setting categories (Appearance, Scanning, Data, Shortcuts, About) with icons; clicking one swaps the right pane to just that group's controls. A search box at top filters across all settings and jumps to matches. The right pane shows one focused group at a time with breathing room.
ui_patterns.why_not_flat: PortPilot's Settings is one scroll of stacked bordered boxes (Theme/Preferences/Data) with no sub-nav, the same flatness problem in miniature. A category rail gives settings a navigable spine and room to grow (shortcuts, agent config, web-portal auth) without becoming a longer scroll.

ui_patterns.pattern: Unify 'my registered apps' and 'live ports' into one reconciled list with a binding indicator (IDE run/debug panels, PM2/pm2 ls, Docker desktop showing image-vs-running)
ui_patterns.description: Instead of two tabs, one list where each registered app row shows its live state inline: a green dot + ':3000' + 'uptime 12m' when running, or a greyed 'Start' affordance when not. Unmanaged live ports that don't map to any registered app appear in a separate 'Unregistered / discovered' group below, each with an 'Adopt as app' action.
ui_patterns.why_not_flat: PortPilot splits 'My Apps' and 'Active Ports' across two disconnected tabs, so answering 'is my app running and on which port' requires cross-referencing two views. Reconciling them gives one source of truth where managed and discovered states share a row, and the unregistered group is exactly where the OS-noise can live, deprioritized.

steal_these.idea: Three-group collapsible Active Ports list: 'My dev servers' (apps you registered / non-system user ports), 'Other user ports' (unrecognized but user-owned), 'System ports' (svchost/System/PID 4, collapsed by default). Each header: label + count badge + collapse chevron + 'kill group' on hover.
steal_these.how: Classify each scanned port at render time: matches a registered app OR a known dev-port range (3000-9000) and a known runtime (node/python/etc) -> 'My dev servers'; owned by SYSTEM/svchost/well-known OS ports (135/139/445/5040 etc) -> 'System ports', start collapsed; everything else -> 'Other'. This is the single highest-leverage fix: it directly dissolves the 33-box wall by quarantining the OS noise the brief calls out.

steal_these.idea: Switch Active Ports from a 2-column card grid to a sortable single-column table (Status dot | :Port | Process | PID | Command-truncated | actions-on-hover), with click-to-sort column headers.
steal_these.how: Reuse the existing fields but lay them out as aligned columns at ~26px row height; default sort by port ascending within each group. Actions (copy, kill) collapse to hover-revealed icons at row-right instead of always-on per card. Fits all 33 on one screen and lets the eye scan the port column vertically.

steal_these.idea: Status as a leading colored dot + word in every row across both ports and apps.
steal_these.how: green/running, grey/stopped, amber/starting or port-conflict, red/error. Put it in column 1 everywhere (active-ports table, my-apps list, and feed the same count into the VS Code 'PP: N running' status-bar item and web portal). Gives PortPilot a status concept it currently lacks and makes problems scannable as a vertical colour strip.

steal_these.idea: Pin/favourite a port or app to a sticky top band that survives rescans.
steal_these.how: Add a star on row hover; pinned items render in a thin 'Pinned' section above the groups with a subtle tint. Persist pin state in the shared JSON config so it holds across the desktop app, VS Code tree, and web portal. Lets the user float their 2-3 real servers above ephemeral churn.

steal_these.idea: Master-detail: clicking a port/app row opens a right-side inspector with the full (untruncated) command, cwd, PID, uptime, copy buttons, and a guarded Kill.
steal_these.how: Keep the list rows light (just enough to identify/rank). Move PROCESS/PID/full-COMMAND and copy/kill into the inspector panel. This removes the per-card overload and finally gives the truncated command line full width to be read and copied.

steal_these.idea: Reconcile My Apps and Active Ports into one view: registered apps show live port + status inline; truly unregistered live ports sit in a discovered group with 'Adopt as app'.
steal_these.how: Join on port/PID between the registered-apps config and the live scan. A registered app that's running shows its green dot and live ':3000'; an unmapped dev port offers one-click registration. Collapses two disconnected tabs into one answer to 'is my app up and where'.

steal_these.idea: Replace top-tab navigation with a left icon rail (Ports, Apps, Knowledge, Settings) and convert Settings into a category-list + detail layout.
steal_these.how: A vertical left rail scales past 5 destinations without eating horizontal-card space and mirrors the VS Code activity-bar mental model users already have from the extension. Inside Settings, a sub-rail (Appearance/Scanning/Data/Shortcuts/About) swaps a focused right pane, ending the flat stack of bordered boxes.

steal_these.idea: Filter chips + remembered default view above the list ('Mine', 'Listening', 'Node', 'System', 'Conflicts' + sort-by).
steal_these.how: Upgrade the lone filter text box into search + one-tap category chips + a sort dropdown, and persist the last-used combo in the JSON config so the user lands on 'Mine, by port' every launch instead of re-filtering a 33-item wall.

status_visualization: The reference tools converge on a leading colored status dot (green=running, grey=stopped/exited, amber=starting/conflict, red=error) reinforced by a short state word so it never relies on colour alone, always pinned to column 1 so a vertical scan of the dots locates the one problem among 30 healthy rows. At the group level, headers carry an aggregate pill like Docker's 'Running (3/4)' that rolls child states up so a collapsed section still reports health. Conflict/clash (two things fighting for a port) should get its own amber/red treatment with an icon, since that is PortPilot's most actionable bad state and currently has no representation. The same single running-count must feed the desktop list, the VS Code 'PP: N running' status-bar item, and the web portal so all three surfaces agree.
density_and_hierarchy: Density comes from (1) abandoning the 2-column card grid for a ~26px-row sortable table, which roughly triples on-screen item count and aligns attributes into scannable columns; (2) collapsible counted group headers that fold the list from O(33 items) to O(3-6 groups), with the OS-noise group collapsed by default; (3) master-detail, which moves heavy fields (full command, cwd, logs) out of the list into an on-demand inspector so list rows stay light; (4) pinned/sticky bands that give important items a stable spatial home. At PortPilot's ~33-item scale virtualization is unnecessary (it matters past ~hundreds of rows) - the win is grouping + table density, not windowing. Hierarchy is created by three altitudes: group header (census + bulk action), row (identify + rank + quick action), inspector (full detail), replacing today's single overloaded altitude.
caveats: Do not copy heavyweight process-tool chrome wholesale: Activity Monitor's 5 resource tabs, live CPU/memory/network sparklines, and customizable-column managers are overkill for a localhost port tool and would re-bloat the UI - PortPilot has no meaningful per-process CPU/mem story to tell. Skip virtualization (react-window etc.); at ~33 rows it adds complexity and scroll-jank risk for zero benefit. Don't over-engineer saved-views/segments into a full Linear-style view system - one remembered default filter is plenty for v1. Auto-classification of 'system vs dev' must be conservative and overridable (a manual 'move to group' / pin escape hatch) because heuristics will mislabel edge cases, and silently hiding a port the user needs is worse than showing noise. Keep the master-detail inspector dismissible/optional so quick kill-a-port flows don't require a two-click drill-in - surface kill on row hover too. Finally, the left-rail nav and three-group model must be implemented once and shared by all three surfaces via the common JSON config, or the redesign just moves the flatness problem between surfaces.
applicability_reason: These tools (Docker Desktop's collapsible compose groups, Activity Monitor's system/user process split, and the table-over-cards convention of every serious process manager) are an almost one-to-one structural match for PortPilot's exact failure - a uniform grid mixing OS ports with dev servers - so the grouping, signal/noise, and table patterns transfer directly with minimal adaptation.
